bio: A young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, who is told by the angel Gabriel that she will bear the Son of the Most High. Luke gives her song, the Magnificat. She is with Jesus at the wedding at Cana and stands near the cross, where he entrusts her to the beloved disciple. In Acts 1:14 she is with the believers in the upper room.
rel: Wife of Joseph; relative of Elizabeth

bio: A builder (Greek tekton, often rendered “carpenter”) from Nazareth, a descendant of David. In Matthew he obeys dreams to take Mary as his wife, to flee to Egypt and to settle in Nazareth. He disappears from the story after Jesus is twelve.
rel: Husband of Mary

bio: Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, he preached repentance in the Judean wilderness and baptized in the Jordan. He pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, rebuked Herod Antipas for his marriage and was beheaded at Machaerus.
rel: Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth; relative of Mary

bio: An elderly priest of the course of Abijah who is struck silent when Gabriel announces John’s birth in the Temple. His speech returns at the naming of the child, when he sings the Benedictus.
rel: Husband of Elizabeth

bio: A relative of Mary from a priestly family, who conceives in old age. When Mary visits, the child leaps in her womb and she blesses Mary as “the mother of my Lord”.
rel: Wife of Zechariah; relative of Mary

bio: The angel who stands in God’s presence, who announces the births of John and Jesus. He also appears in Daniel.
A devout man in Jerusalem who was promised he would see the Messiah. He takes the baby Jesus in his arms and speaks the Nunc Dimittis, warning Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul.
An elderly widow of the tribe of Asher who worshipped night and day in the Temple. She thanks God at the sight of the child and speaks of him to all who await redemption.
The first Roman emperor. Luke dates Jesus’ birth to a census decreed in his reign. Herod the Great ruled Judea as his client king.
Augustus’s successor, in whose fifteenth year (about AD 28–29) John began to preach. His image was on the silver denarius of Jesus’ question about taxes.

A brilliant, brutal builder who rebuilt the Temple, the fortresses of Masada and Herodium, and the port of Caesarea. Matthew shows him trying to kill the child Jesus after the visit of the Magi. He died in 4 BC.
rel: Father of Antipas

sub: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, 4 BC – AD 39
bio: A son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee through Jesus’ whole ministry. He founded Tiberias, imprisoned and killed John the Baptist, and questioned Jesus before the crucifixion. Jesus called him “that fox”.
rel: Husband of Herodias; son of Herod the Great

bio: A granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her first husband, Antipas’s half-brother, to marry Antipas. John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and she arranged his death.
rel: Wife of Antipas

bio: The Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to be crucified. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and provocative. A building inscription found at Caesarea names him “Prefect of Judea”. First Timothy 6:13 speaks of “Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.”

Joseph Caiaphas was high priest through Jesus’ ministry and presided over the trial before the Sanhedrin. A richly decorated ossuary found in Jerusalem in 1990 is inscribed with his family name. In Acts he is among the rulers who question Peter and John (4:6).
rel: Son-in-law of Annas

bio: The powerful former high priest (AD 6–15) whose sons and son-in-law held the office after him. John says Jesus was taken to him first. In Acts he is named with Caiaphas as high priest (4:6).
rel: Father-in-law of Caiaphas

bio: A fisherman from Bethsaida who lived at Capernaum, brother of Andrew. Jesus renames him “Peter” (the Rock). He confesses Jesus as the Christ, denies him three times, and is restored on the shore of the lake after the resurrection. In Acts he leads the Jerusalem church: he preaches at Pentecost, heals a lame man, stands before the council, takes the gospel to Cornelius, and is freed from prison by an angel. Paul calls him Cephas in 1 Corinthians. Some at Corinth said “I follow Cephas.” Paul lists him first among those to whom the risen Christ appeared (15:5) and notes that he travels with a believing wife (9:5). In Galatians Paul calls him Cephas. He stayed with him for fifteen days (1:18), is among the “pillars” in Jerusalem (2:9), and at Antioch was opposed “to his face” for drawing back from the Gentiles (2:11-14). The first letter of Peter opens “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1) and presents him in chapter 5 as “a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed” (5:1). He says he writes from “Babylon” (5:13), which many early writers took to mean Rome. Clement of Rome (about AD 96) and later writers say Peter was put to death there. The letter has many echoes of the sayings and acts of Jesus that Peter had known, among them the Chief Shepherd (John 21:15-17) and the stone the builders rejected (Mark 12:10). The second letter that bears his name opens “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:1), and has him say that “the tent of my body” will soon be laid aside (1:13-14), as the Lord had made clear to him. Many scholars doubt that he wrote it himself, and think someone wrote it in his name after his death; others hold that he wrote it near the end of his life. The letter says he was an eyewitness of Christ’s majesty on the holy mountain (1:16-18).
rel: Brother of Andrew

bio: A former disciple of John the Baptist who first followed Jesus and brought his brother Peter to him. He brings the boy with loaves and fish and brings Greeks to Jesus.
rel: Brother of Peter

bio: Fishermen partnered with Peter, nicknamed “Sons of Thunder”. With Peter they are the inner circle at the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. Herod Agrippa I executed James around AD 44. In Acts, John goes with Peter to the temple and to Samaria. Herod Agrippa kills James with the sword (12:2), the first of the Twelve to die. Paul names “John” among the pillars who gave him the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9).
rel: Sons of Zebedee and probably Salome

bio: Called on the day after Andrew and Peter. He brings Nathanael to Jesus, is asked where to buy bread for the five thousand and asks to see the Father at the Last Supper. He is named in the list of the eleven in Acts 1:13.
Brought by Philip and astonished that Jesus saw him under the fig tree. He is named at the end of John among the disciples at the lakeshore. Many identify him with the apostle Bartholomew.
A customs agent at Capernaum who left his booth to follow Jesus and hosted a dinner for tax collectors and sinners. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

Called “the Twin”. He is ready to die with Jesus in John 11, asks “how can we know the way?” and refuses to believe in the resurrection until he sees the marks of the nails, then declares “My Lord and my God!”

The disciples’ treasurer, who agreed to hand Jesus over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. Matthew says he returned the silver and hanged himself. Acts 1 tells how he died and how Matthias took his place.
A woman from Magdala whom Jesus had freed of seven demons. She supported his ministry, stood at the cross and was the first to see the risen Lord.
She sat at Jesus’ feet to listen while Martha served. John says she poured expensive perfume on his feet six days before Passover.
rel: Sister of Martha and Lazarus

bio: Hosted Jesus at Bethany and made the confession “I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” John 11 pictures her meeting Jesus on the road after her brother’s death.
rel: Sister of Mary and Lazarus

bio: Raised from the tomb after four days. The raising prompts the plot to kill Jesus. His tomb is shown at Bethany today. (The poor man in Luke’s parable has the same name but is a different character.)
rel: Brother of Martha and Mary

bio: A woman of means, wife of Chuza, a manager of Herod Antipas’s household, who supported Jesus out of her own funds and was at the empty tomb.
Named by Mark among the women at the cross and the tomb. She is probably the “mother of the sons of Zebedee” in Matthew’s list, who asks Jesus for places for her sons.
rel: Probably mother of James and John

sub: Pharisee and member of the council
bio: He comes to Jesus by night, speaks up for him before the council, and after the crucifixion brings about a hundred pounds of spices for the burial.
A rich, righteous member of the council who did not consent to Jesus’ condemnation. He asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb.

A short, wealthy toll official who climbed a sycamore-fig to see Jesus. Jesus invited himself to his house, and Zacchaeus promised to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated.
A leader of a synagogue, probably at Capernaum, who begged Jesus to come and heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter. Jesus raised her up.
Mark names him “son of Timaeus”. He called out to the “Son of David,” was healed and followed Jesus on the road. Matthew mentions two blind men; Luke does not give a name.
A non-Jewish officer, likely in Herod Antipas’s service, who built the local synagogue. He asked Jesus to heal his servant and said “just say the word.” Jesus marveled at his faith.
A Greek woman of Syrian Phoenicia whose daughter was oppressed by a demon. She pressed Jesus to help, saying even the dogs eat the children’s crumbs. Matthew calls her a Canaanite.
A woman who came to draw water at noon at Sychar. Jesus told her about living water and about worship in spirit and truth; she became the first witness to the Samaritans.

sub: Healed in the country of the Gerasenes
bio: A man living among the tombs, with so many spirits that they called themselves “Legion”. After he was healed, Jesus sent him home to tell his own people, and he proclaimed it across the Decapolis.
A widow whose only son was being carried out of the village for burial when Jesus touched the bier and told him to rise.

sub: Healed at the Pool of Siloam
bio: Jesus makes mud, applies it to the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. His healing leads to a debate with the Pharisees and his own parents.
He lay by the pool with the sick, and Jesus told him to take up his mat and walk. The healing was on a Sabbath.
She put two small copper coins (lepta) into the Temple treasury. Jesus said she had given more than all the rest, because she gave out of her poverty.

sub: Man who asked about eternal life
bio: A wealthy man who had kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus loved him and told him to sell his possessions and follow; he went away grieving.
A man in prison for insurrection and murder. At the Passover amnesty the crowd chose him over Jesus.
A man from the Jewish community of Cyrene, in modern Libya, pressed by the soldiers to carry Jesus’ cross. Mark calls him the father of Alexander and Rufus.

sub: Disciple on the road to Emmaus
bio: One of two followers who walked from Jerusalem on Easter afternoon and failed to recognize Jesus until he broke bread with them.
The officer who watched Jesus die and said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

Cited for the Law, the bronze serpent, the manna and the commandment about divorce. He appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration. In Acts 3:22 and 7:20-44 Moses is a prophet like Jesus. Paul says death reigned “from Adam until Moses” (5:14), recalls God’s word to Moses about mercy (9:15), and cites Moses on the righteousness that comes from the law (10:5, 19). Paul says the forefathers “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2) and quotes “the Law of Moses” about the ox (9:9). In 2 Corinthians 3:7-16 Paul uses the veil over Moses’ face to show the difference between the old covenant and the new. Ephesians 6:2-3 quotes the fifth commandment given at Sinai, “Honor your father and mother,” which Paul calls “the first commandment with a promise.” In 2 Timothy 3:8 Paul says “Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.” Hebrews 3:1-6 says Moses was faithful “as a servant” in God’s house, and Christ as a Son over it. Chapter 8 says that Moses was warned to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (8:5). Chapter 11 tells how Moses’ parents hid him, how he chose to suffer oppression with God’s people, and how he kept the Passover (11:23-28). Jude 9 refers to a Jewish story in which the archangel Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses.” Deuteronomy 34:6 says that no one knows where Moses was buried. In Revelation 15:3 those who have conquered the beast sing “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb.” One of the two witnesses of chapter 11 has the powers Moses used in Egypt.

The prophet who was expected to return before the Day of the Lord. Jesus says John the Baptist is that Elijah, and Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration. Paul recalls Elijah’s complaint and God’s reply about the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal (Romans 11:2-4). James 5:17-18 says that Elijah “was a man just like us.” He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years, and then he prayed again and the heavens gave rain. James uses him as proof that “the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.” One of the two witnesses of Revelation 11 has Elijah’s powers: fire, and shutting the sky so that no rain falls.

The patriarch of Genesis. Jesus’ opponents claim him as their father; Jesus says he saw Abraham’s day and, “Before Abraham was, I am.” In Acts 3:25 and 7:2-8 Peter and Stephen speak of Abraham. Romans 4 argues that Abraham was credited with righteousness by faith before he was circumcised, so that he is father of all who believe. Galatians 3 argues from Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6), “those who have faith are sons of Abraham” (3:7), and the blessing comes to the Gentiles in him (3:8-9). In chapter 4 Paul reads the story of his two sons as a picture of two covenants. Hebrews 6:13-18 says that when God made a promise to Abraham he swore by himself. In chapter 7 Abraham gives a tenth to Melchizedek and is blessed by him, which shows that Melchizedek is greater. In chapter 11 he obeys the call without knowing where he is going, lives in tents, and is ready to offer Isaac (11:8-19). James 2:21-23 appeals to Abraham twice: he was “justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar,” and the Scripture that says “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” was fulfilled, and he was called a friend of God.

Israel’s great king, ancestor of the Messiah. The title “Son of David” appears often; archaeology offers the Tel Dan stele’s mention of the “House of David”. In Acts, Peter and Paul read the Psalms as David’s words about the Messiah. Romans 4 quotes David on the blessing of the person whose sin is not counted (Psalm 32), and Romans 11 quotes his curse on those who stumbled (Psalm 69). In 2 Timothy 2:8 Paul tells Timothy to remember Jesus Christ, “raised from the dead, descended from David.” Hebrews 4:7 says that God speaks “through David” in Psalm 95, and Psalm 110, quoted in chapters 1, 5 and 7, is also a psalm of David. David is named in the list of the faithful (11:32). In Revelation Jesus holds “the key of David” (3:7) and is “the Root of David” (5:5) and “the Root and the Offspring of David” (22:16).

The prophet Jesus quotes most. Luke has him read from the Isaiah scroll in the Nazareth synagogue, and the Gospels cite him for John the Baptist’s ministry. In Acts, Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian, and Paul closes by quoting Isaiah 6. Paul quotes Isaiah more than any other prophet in Romans, on the remnant (9:27-29), the stone of stumbling (9:33), the beautiful feet of the messengers (10:15) and the root of Jesse (15:12). Ephesians 2:17 echoes Isaiah’s words about “peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Isaiah 57:19; 52:7), and the armor of 6:14-17 borrows from Isaiah 11:5, 52:7 and 59:17. A Jewish tradition says that Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, and some readers think this is behind Hebrews 11:37, which speaks of those who were “sawed in two.” The Old Testament does not record how Isaiah died.
Jesus calls his own resurrection after three days “the sign of Jonah” and says the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching.

The builder of the first Temple, celebrated for wisdom and splendor. Jesus says the lilies are more beautiful and that “something greater than Solomon is here”. In Acts 7:47 Stephen says Solomon built the house, yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands.

The adversary who tempts Jesus in the wilderness, and whom Jesus pictures falling like lightning as God’s kingdom advances. The name means “accuser”. In 2 Corinthians Paul does not want to be outwitted by him (2:11), calls him “the god of this age” who “has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (4:4), says he “masquerades as an angel of light” (11:14), and links him to the “messenger of Satan” that torments Paul (12:7). Ephesians speaks of “the ruler of the power of the air” (2:2), warns “do not give the devil a foothold” (4:27), and tells believers to “make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (6:11). It also speaks of “all the flaming arrows of the evil one” (6:16). In 1 Thessalonians Paul says “Satan obstructed us” from coming back to the church (2:18) and fears “the tempter” had tempted them (3:5). In the second letter the coming of the lawless one is “accompanied by the working of Satan” (2 Thessalonians 2:9), and the Lord will “guard you from the evil one” (3:3). In 1 Timothy Paul says he has “handed over to Satan” Hymenaeus and Alexander (1:20). A new convert may “fall under the same condemnation as the devil” (3:6), and “some have already turned aside to follow Satan” (5:15). In 2 Timothy 2:26 Paul hopes that opponents will “escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.” Hebrews 2:14-15 says that Christ shared flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy “him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil” and free those held in slavery by the fear of death. James 4:7 tells the readers to “resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” In 2:19 even the demons believe in one God “and shudder,” and in 3:15 the wisdom that comes from jealousy and selfish ambition is called “earthly, unspiritual, demonic.” In 1 Peter 5:8 he is “your adversary the devil,” who “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” Peter tells the readers to be “sober-minded and alert” and to resist him, “standing firm in your faith” (5:9). 1 John 3:8 says “The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil.” The letter also speaks of “the evil one” (2:13-14; 3:12; 5:18-19) and says “the whole world is under the power of the evil one” (5:19). In Jude 9 the archangel Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses” and left the rebuke to the Lord. Revelation names him fully: “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9). He is thrown out of heaven, bound for a thousand years, and finally thrown into the lake of fire (20:10). Pergamum is “where the throne of Satan sits” (2:13).

Twelve men appointed to be with Jesus and to be sent out, matching the twelve tribes of Israel. The four lists in the New Testament differ slightly in the order and minor names. In Acts the eleven choose Matthias, then stand with Peter at Pentecost and lead the church until the Seven are chosen.

sub: Teachers who stressed the oral tradition
bio: A lay movement that stressed purity, tithing, Sabbath-keeping and the “tradition of the elders”. They were respected among ordinary people and clashed with Jesus over Sabbath, table fellowship and authority. In Acts Gamaliel, a Pharisee, advises caution; some Pharisees join the church and argue for circumcision (15:5); Paul says he is a Pharisee (23:6; 26:5). In Philippians 3:5-6 Paul says he was “as to the law, a Pharisee,” “as to zeal, persecuting the church,” and “as to righteousness in the law, faultless.”

A group of wealthy priestly families that controlled the Temple and accepted only the written Torah. They denied the resurrection and the existence of angels. In Acts they arrest Peter and John because they teach the resurrection (4:1-2), and they divide from the Pharisees at Paul’s hearing.
Professional teachers and copyists of Scripture, also called lawyers or teachers of the law. Many belonged to the Pharisees.

The ruling body in Jerusalem, made up of the high priest, senior priests, elders and scribes. It could try cases but needed Rome’s approval to carry out an execution. In Acts the council arrests the apostles, tries Stephen, and hears Paul. Saul carries letters from the chief priest to Damascus.
Political backers of the Herod family. They are named only twice together with the Pharisees, plotting against Jesus.
Local men who bid for the right to collect tolls and customs, often for a share of the money. Hated as collaborators and extortioners, they are often grouped with “sinners” in the Gospels.

sub: Neighbors of the Jews, kin of Israel
bio: Descendants of the northern kingdom’s people, with their own temple on Mount Gerizim and their own Torah. Jews and Samaritans were bitter rivals, which is why Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan startled his listeners. In Acts Philip preaches in Samaria and many believe; Peter and John come down and the Spirit is given.

Rome ruled Judea through a prefect and auxiliary troops stationed in Caesarea and in Jerusalem’s Antonia fortress. Soldiers appear as the centurion, the Gethsemane arrest party, the mocking guard and those who cast lots for the clothing. In Acts, Roman officers include the centurion Cornelius, the tribune Lysias, the governors Felix and Festus, and the centurion Julius. In Ephesians 6:10-17 Paul describes God’s armor in terms of a Roman soldier’s gear. He was under their guard when he wrote (Acts 28:16, 20).
Hired and family shepherds who lived outdoors near Bethlehem and across Judea and Galilee. In Luke, they are the first to hear the birth announcement.

Learned men from the east, likely astrologers from Persia or Babylon, who followed a star to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem with gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. Matthew does not give a number.

Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women who funded Jesus’ ministry. They were present at the crucifixion and discovered the empty tomb. In Acts 1:14 the women are with the eleven in the upper room.

A fertile, densely settled region ruled by Herod Antipas. Most of Jesus’ ministry took place here, among villages around the lake and on the road between Tiberias and Sepphoris. In Acts 9:31 the church has peace in Judea, Galilee and Samaria.

The southern region, ruled directly by a Roman prefect from AD 6. It includes Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Bethany, Jericho and the wilderness. In Acts “all Judea” hears the word and the church is scattered through it. Paul says the Thessalonians “became imitators of the churches of God in Judea” (1 Thessalonians 2:14).

The hill country of the old northern kingdom. Pilgrims often detoured east through the Jordan Valley to avoid it, but Jesus goes through. In Acts it is the second ring of the mission: “Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

A group of ten cities, mostly east of the Jordan, with Greek culture and pagan temples. Scythopolis (Beth Shean) was the only one west of the river. Jesus visits the region and sends a healed man to proclaim the good news there.
The strip of land east of the Jordan, ruled by Antipas. It contained Machaerus, where John was killed, and the place where John had baptized.

Two ancient Phoenician ports in what is now Lebanon, outside Herod’s territory. People from these cities came to hear Jesus, and he withdrew there at one point. In Acts Paul lands at Tyre and finds disciples, and later his ship calls at Sidon.

A large Jewish community lived in Egypt, especially in Alexandria. Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child there to escape Herod and later returned to Nazareth. Coptic tradition places their stay around Old Cairo. In Acts 7 Stephen retells the stories of Joseph and Moses in Egypt. The story of Jannes and Jambres, Pharaoh’s magicians, is set here (2 Timothy 3:8). Jude 5 reminds its readers that the people were “delivered” “out of the land of Egypt,” and that those who did not believe were afterward destroyed.
A small farming village in the lower Galilean hills, probably a few hundred people, near the larger city of Sepphoris. Excavations show terraced fields, wine presses and simple houses.

sub: Town of David, six miles south of Jerusalem
bio: A small village in Judea, linked to David and to Micah’s prophecy of a ruler from there. The Church of the Nativity stands over a grotto honored since the 2nd century.

A fishing and farming village on the north shore, with a customs post and a Roman garrison nearby. Jesus taught in its synagogue and healed in Peter’s house. Excavations show black basalt houses and a later white limestone synagogue.
The site of Jesus’ first sign at a wedding and a later healing. Two villages claim the name, Kafr Kanna (traditional) and Khirbet Qana, which has more first-century remains.
A small village on the slope of the Hill of Moreh, where Jesus raised a widow’s son. The village still exists as Nein.

sub: Fishing village near the lake’s north end
bio: The home of Peter, Andrew and Philip. It lay just east of the Jordan in Philip’s territory and was rebuilt as a Greek-style city. The leading candidate is et-Tell.
A basalt town two miles north of Capernaum. Jesus names it with Bethsaida as a city that saw his deeds and did not repent.

sub: Fishing town on the western shore
bio: The home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations have uncovered a first-century synagogue with a carved stone, a market, a harbor and ritual baths. Matthew calls the place Magadan.
A rich crescent of farmland between Magdala and Capernaum, which gave the lake one of its names. Jesus landed here after walking on water, and crowds brought him the sick.

sub: Pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon
bio: Philip’s capital, built near a spring and a cave shrine of the god Pan. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ in this region.
A gentile district east of the lake, with a steep bank beside the water. The Gospels name it differently (Gerasa, Gadara, Gergesa), perhaps because the area was linked to more than one city.

sub: Oasis city in the Jordan Valley
bio: One of the oldest cities in the world. Herod built a winter palace on the new site, about two miles from the ancient mound. Jesus heals the blind and visits Zacchaeus here on his way up to Jerusalem.

sub: Village on the Mount of Olives
bio: Home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, about two miles east of Jerusalem. Jesus stays here during Passion Week.

sub: Village near the Mount of Olives
bio: The village where Jesus sent two disciples to find a colt for his entry into Jerusalem.
Where the risen Jesus broke bread with two disciples. Its location is uncertain, and several sites have been proposed.
A Samaritan village below Mount Gerizim. Jacob’s Well, honored since early times, is the setting for the long talk with the Samaritan woman.

The city whose destruction becomes Jesus’ standard for judgement. Its location is debated, but traditions place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea. 2 Peter 2:6 says God condemned “the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly.” Jude 7 says that “Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them” are “on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.”
The great Assyrian city on the Tigris, to which Jonah was sent. Jesus holds up its people as examples of repentance.

sub: Freshwater lake, also Gennesaret and Tiberias
bio: About 13 miles long and 8 wide and nearly 700 feet below sea level. It is a harp-shaped lake that supported a fishing industry, with sudden storms funneled down by the hills.
Flows from Mount Hermon through the lake and down to the Dead Sea. John baptized on it, and two sites, Qasr al-Yahud and Al-Maghtas, claim Jesus’ baptism.

sub: Dry hills between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea
bio: A rocky desert of limestone ridges and canyons. John preached here, Jesus fasted here, and the Qumran community withdrew to its edge.
Matthew sets the Sermon on “the mountain” and Luke on “a level place”. Tradition places it on the northern hills above Tabgha, where the Church of the Beatitudes now stands.

The Gospels say only that Jesus took three disciples up “a high mountain”. Tradition since the 4th century says Mount Tabor, while some scholars prefer Mount Hermon. 2 Peter 1:18 recalls the voice from heaven “when we were with Him on the holy mountain,” which most take to be the Transfiguration.

A city of perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, packed with pilgrims at festivals, built on two ridges around the Temple Mount. It lay about 2,500 feet above sea level, and Gospel writers often say people “go up” to it. In Acts it is the home of the first church, the city of the council, and the place where Paul is arrested. Paul is about to take the collection from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28). The Corinthians are to set aside money each week for the saints in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-3). In 2 Corinthians 8-9 Paul asks the Corinthians to finish the gift for the poor believers here. In Galatians Paul went up here after three years, and again after fourteen years. He also contrasts “the present-day Jerusalem” with “the Jerusalem above” (4:25-26).

The great sanctuary rebuilt by Herod the Great on a vast platform, with courts for Gentiles, women, Israel and priests. Jesus teaches here, drives out the merchants and predicts its destruction, which came in AD 70. In Acts the believers meet daily in the temple courts, Peter heals a lame man at the gate, and Paul is seized there. Ephesians 2:19-22 says believers are being built together “into a holy temple in the Lord,” “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.” The letter also says the “dividing wall” has been removed (2:14).

A ridge across the Kidron Valley from the Temple, where Jesus approached Jerusalem, taught about the end, prayed on the night of his arrest and, in Acts, ascended. In Acts 1:12 the apostles return from this mountain after the Ascension. Ephesians 4:8-10 speaks of Christ who “ascended on high” and who also “descended to the lower parts of the earth,” using words from Psalm 68. The Mount of Olives is where Acts 1:9-12 places the ascension.
An olive press and garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives. The name means “oil press”. Jesus prayed here and was arrested.
An Aramaic name meaning “skull”, where Jesus was crucified outside the city walls. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands on the traditional site.
A double pool with five colonnades near the Sheep Gate, excavated north of the Temple Mount. A man waited here thirty-eight years.

sub: Pool at the south end of the city
bio: A large stepped pool at the end of Hezekiah’s tunnel, where pilgrims purified themselves. The blind man washed here.

The Spirit descends on Jesus at his baptism and leads him into the wilderness. In John, Jesus promises the Spirit as a Helper who will teach the disciples and remind them of all he has said. In Acts the Spirit comes at Pentecost, fills the believers, falls on Samaritans and Gentiles, sends Barnabas and Saul, and guides the mission step by step. Romans 8 is the fullest teaching on the Spirit in Paul: the Spirit gives life, leads God’s children and prays for believers. In 1 Corinthians the Spirit searches all things, “even the deep things of God” (2:10), dwells in the believer’s body as in a temple (6:19), and gives gifts to each “for the common good” (12:7). In 2 Corinthians the Spirit is the “pledge of what is to come” (1:22), writes on hearts “not with ink” (3:3), and “gives life” (3:6). “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (3:17), and the letter ends with “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (13:14). In Galatians the Spirit is received “by hearing with faith” (3:2), sent into hearts crying “Abba, Father” (4:6), and produces fruit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (5:22-23). Paul says “Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit” (5:25). In Ephesians believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13) and have access to the Father “by one Spirit” (2:18). Paul prays that they be strengthened “with power through His Spirit” (3:16), urges them to keep “the unity of the Spirit” (4:3), warns “do not grieve the Holy Spirit” (4:30), says “be filled with the Spirit” (5:18), and calls the Word “the sword of the Spirit” (6:17). Second Timothy 1:14 says to guard the treasure “with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us,” and 1:7 says God has given “a spirit of fear” no place but “of power, love, and self-control.” Titus 3:5-6 speaks of “renewal by the Holy Spirit” and says God “poured out” the Spirit “abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.” In 1 John he is the anointing that “remains in you” (2:27), the proof that God remains in us: “by the Spirit He has given us” (3:24). The letter names “the Spirit of truth” (4:6) against “the spirit of deception,” and says the Spirit, the water and the blood testify together (5:6-8). Jude tells his readers to keep on “praying in the Holy Spirit” (Jude 20), and says the intruders are “devoid of the Spirit” (Jude 19). In Revelation John is “in the Spirit” when he sees his visions (1:10; 4:2), every letter ends with “what the Spirit says to the churches” (2:7), and at the close “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (22:17). The “seven Spirits before His throne” (1:4) are usually taken as the one Spirit in his fullness.

Mark and Matthew name four brothers and mention sisters. The Gospels say they did not believe in him during his ministry. James later led the Jerusalem church. In Acts 1:14 they are with the believers, and James leads the Jerusalem church. The letter of Jude is written by “a brother of James” (Jude 1), by the usual reading the Judas of Mark 6:3. Hegesippus tells of grandsons of Jude who farmed in the land of Israel late in the first century.

A large furnished room in Jerusalem where Jesus ate the Passover meal with his disciples, washed their feet and gave the long farewell talk in John 13–17. The tradition on Mount Zion is old, but the actual house is unknown. In Acts 1:13 the believers stay in an upper room, and wait for the Spirit.

A Jew born in Tarsus, trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and a Roman citizen. As Saul he approves Stephen’s death and arrests believers, until the risen Jesus meets him on the road to Damascus. He then takes the gospel to Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece in three journeys, is arrested at the temple, appeals to Caesar, and reaches Rome in chains. In Romans he writes as an apostle who has not yet been to Rome, explains the gospel for Jew and Gentile, and describes his plans for Jerusalem and Spain. In 1 Corinthians he answers a church he founded, writing from Ephesus. He calls himself the one who laid the foundation, tells how he works with his hands, and says he became “all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.” In 2 Corinthians he writes from Macedonia after a painful visit, a sharp letter and a long wait for Titus. He defends his ministry, lists his sufferings, tells of his escape from Damascus and of a thorn in the flesh, and says “when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10). In Galatians he opens with “an apostle—sent not from men nor by man” (1:1), tells how he came to the gospel and met the Jerusalem leaders, and confronts Peter at Antioch. He then argues for faith over works of the law, writes with “large letters” in his “own hand” (6:11), and says “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (6:17). In Ephesians he calls himself “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1) and “the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (3:1). He says he is “less than the least of all the saints” (3:8), and asks the readers to pray that he will speak boldly, “an ambassador in chains” (6:19-20). In Philippians he writes with Timothy as “servants of Christ Jesus” (1:1), is in chains (1:7, 13), and says, “to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). He lists his old credentials as a Pharisee and “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (3:5) and counts them as loss (3:7-8). He has “learned to be content regardless of my circumstances” (4:11). In Colossians he writes with Timothy (1:1) to a church he has not met (2:1). He is “a servant” of the gospel (1:23, 25), rejoices in “my sufferings for you” (1:24), asks for prayer for “which I am in chains” (4:3), and ends with a greeting “in my own hand” (4:18). In 1 and 2 Thessalonians he writes with Silvanus and Timothy to a church he had to leave soon after founding it (1 Thessalonians 2:17). He reminds them that he worked “night and day” (2:9), calls himself “like a nursing mother” and “as a father” (2:7, 11), and wrote the closing greeting of the second letter “in my own hand” (2 Thessalonians 3:17). In 1 Timothy he writes to Timothy at Ephesus, as “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior” (1:1). He calls himself “formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man” who “was shown mercy” (1:13), and says Christ came to save sinners, “of whom I am the worst” (1:15). Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote the letter or a later follower did. In 2 Timothy he writes in chains, as “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus” (1:1). He asks Timothy not to be ashamed “of me, His prisoner” (1:8), and says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7). Many take it as his last letter. Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote it or a later follower did. In Titus he is “a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). He tells Titus, “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished” (1:5), and says, “I have decided to winter” at Nicopolis (3:12). Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote it or a later follower wrote in his name. In Philemon he is “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (verse 1) who prefers to “appeal on the basis of love” (verse 9). He writes “with my own hand” (verse 19), promises to repay anything Onesimus owes, and asks for a guest room because he hopes to be “restored” to the church (verse 22). The letter does not say where he was held. 2 Peter 3:15-16 calls him “our beloved brother Paul,” says he wrote to the readers “with the wisdom God gave him,” and adds that “some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures.”
rel: Companion of Barnabas, Silas, Timothy and Luke

bio: A Levite from Cyprus whose given name was Joseph. He sells a field and gives the money to the apostles, vouches for Saul in Jerusalem, brings him to Antioch, and travels with him on the first journey. After a sharp disagreement over John Mark he sails again to Cyprus. Paul mentions Barnabas as one who, like himself, works for a living (1 Corinthians 9:6). In Galatians he goes up to Jerusalem with Paul and Titus (2:1), receives the right hand of fellowship (2:9), and at Antioch is “led astray” with Peter by the hypocrisy of the others (2:13). Colossians 4:10 names Mark as “the cousin of Barnabas.” Tertullian, in the early 200s, named Barnabas as the writer of Hebrews, and some scholars still favor him, since he was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36) and a “son of encouragement,” and Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). The letter does not name its author.
rel: Cousin of John Mark (Colossians 4:10)

sub: First martyr; one of the Seven
bio: A Greek-speaking believer “full of faith and the Holy Spirit,” chosen to serve the widows. Accused before the council, he retells Israel’s history and says the Righteous One has come. He sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand and is stoned, praying for his killers.
rel: One of the Seven

bio: Chosen with Stephen to serve the widows, he preaches in Samaria, explains Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official, and baptizes him. He later lives in Caesarea with four daughters who prophesy, where Paul stays with him.
rel: Father of four daughters who prophesied

bio: A disciple in Damascus, “well spoken of by all the Jews.” The Lord sends him to the street called Straight to lay hands on Saul, who has been blind for three days. Though afraid because of Saul’s reputation, he obeys and calls him “Brother Saul.”

sub: A couple in the Jerusalem church
bio: A husband and wife who sell a piece of property and bring part of the price to the apostles while claiming to give all of it. Peter says they lied to the Holy Spirit; both die, and fear falls on the whole church.
rel: Husband and wife

bio: The high priest who orders Paul struck on the mouth at the council, and who later goes to Caesarea with Tertullus to accuse him before Felix. Josephus names an Ananias son of Nedebaeus as high priest in about AD 47-59.

A centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea, “devout and God-fearing,” who prays and gives to the poor. An angel tells him to send for Peter. When Peter preaches in his house the Holy Spirit falls on his whole household, and they are baptized.
rel: His household and close friends

bio: A man who amazed the Samaritans with magic and who believed and was baptized after Philip’s preaching. When he sees the Spirit given through the apostles’ hands he offers money for the power, and Peter rebukes him.

A eunuch and chief treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, returning from worship in Jerusalem. He is reading Isaiah 53 aloud in his chariot when Philip joins him, explains the passage, and baptizes him in water along the road.
A disciple known for good works and charity, especially the clothing she made for widows. When she dies, the believers send for Peter, who prays, says “Tabitha, arise,” and presents her alive.
A Joppa craftsman whose house is by the sea. Peter lodges with him, sees the vision of the sheet on his roof, and leaves with the men sent from Cornelius.

sub: Pharisee and teacher of the law
bio: A Pharisee honored by all the people. In the council he tells his colleagues to leave the apostles alone, for if this plan is from men it will fail, but if from God they cannot stop it. Paul later says he was trained at his feet.
rel: Teacher of Saul

bio: A prophet who predicts a great famine, and later binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt to show that the Jews of Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him over to the Gentiles.

A brother of Jesus who did not follow him during his ministry but is named a leader in Jerusalem. After Peter leaves, James presides at the council on the Gentiles and later receives Paul and the elders. The letter of James is traditionally his. Paul saw “James, the Lord’s brother” on his first visit (Galatians 1:19) and counts him among the pillars (2:9). The men “from James” at Antioch changed Peter’s table (2:12). The letter of James calls its writer only “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Tradition from early on has taken him to be James the brother of the Lord. Josephus says that he was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62. Some scholars believe the letter was written in his name by a later Christian, and others that it comes from him, perhaps through a secretary who wrote good Greek. The letter of Jude begins, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (Jude 1). James was well enough known that his name alone told readers who Jude was.
rel: Brother of Jesus and of Jude

bio: The son of Mary, whose Jerusalem home hosted the church. He goes with Barnabas and Saul on the first journey but turns back at Perga. Paul refuses to take him again, so Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus. Mark is traditionally the author of the second Gospel. Colossians 4:10 calls him “Mark the cousin of Barnabas” and tells the church, “If he comes to you, welcome him.” Paul writes, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). Philemon 24 calls him one of Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings. Paul and Barnabas had parted over him (Acts 15:37-39), and here he is again with Paul. Peter calls him “my son Mark” (1 Peter 5:13). Early writers such as Papias said that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, and that his Gospel is built on what Peter taught.
rel: Cousin of Barnabas

bio: The servant girl who recognizes Peter’s voice at the gate of Mary’s house and in her joy forgets to open it. The believers, who are praying for him, first say she is out of her mind.

Grandson of Herod the Great and ruler of a kingdom nearly as large as his grandfather’s. He has James killed, jails Peter at Passover, and dies at Caesarea after accepting the cry that his voice was a god’s, not a man’s.
rel: Father of Agrippa II, Bernice and Drusilla

bio: A Roman governor “a man of intelligence” who summons Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God. When Elymas the magician tries to turn him away and is struck blind, the proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
A Jewish false prophet attached to the proconsul. Paul calls him “full of all deceit and fraud” and a son of the devil, and he is struck blind for a time.

A leading man in the Jerusalem church who carries the Council’s letter to Antioch, then goes with Paul on the second journey. He is beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi, and later stays at Berea. Paul names “me and Silvanus and Timothy” as the ones who preached Christ in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19). In 1 and 2 Thessalonians he is “Silvanus,” named with Paul and Timothy in the greeting (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). In 1 Peter 5:12 the apostle writes, “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly.” The phrase may mean that Silvanus carried the letter, wrote it as Peter’s secretary, or both.
rel: Also called Silvanus

bio: A disciple from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father. Paul has him circumcised and takes him along. He travels with Paul and Silas, stays on at Berea, and is later sent to Macedonia from Ephesus. Timothy sends greetings from Corinth in Romans 16:21. Paul calls Timothy “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” and says he has sent him to remind the Corinthians of his way of life. He asks that Timothy “has nothing to fear while he is with you.” He is named with Paul as sender of 2 Corinthians (1:1) and as one who preached in Corinth (1:19). Timothy is named with Paul as a sender of Philippians (1:1). Paul writes, “I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs” (2:20), and says that “as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel” (2:22). He hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon (2:19, 23). Timothy is named with Paul as a sender of Colossians (1:1), “Timothy our brother.” Paul sent Timothy back to Thessalonica “to strengthen and encourage you in your faith” (1 Thessalonians 3:2), and Timothy returned “with the good news about your faith, your love” (3:6). He is named with Paul in both greetings. First Timothy is addressed to “Timothy, my true child in the faith” (1:2), left at Ephesus to deal with false teaching (1:3). Paul tells him, “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers” (4:12), to “fight the good fight” (1:18; 6:12), and to “guard what has been entrusted” to him (6:20). Second Timothy calls him “my beloved child” (1:2), recalls “your tears” (1:4) and tells him to “fan into flame the gift of God” (1:6), to “be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2:1) and to “Preach the word” (4:2). Paul asks him to “make every effort to come to me quickly” (4:9) and “before winter” (4:21). Philemon 1 names him as co-sender: “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother.” Hebrews 13:23 says “our brother Timothy” has been released and that the writer will come with him if he arrives soon. This is usually taken to be Paul’s coworker, but the letter says nothing more.
rel: Son of Eunice

bio: A God-fearing woman from Thyatira who deals in purple cloth. At a riverside prayer meeting in Philippi ’the Lord opened her heart,’ and she and her household are baptized. She then hosts Paul and his companions.

Wakened at midnight by an earthquake, he sees the doors open and draws his sword to kill himself, until Paul calls out that all are there. He asks, “What must I do to be saved?” and is baptized that night with his household.

A man who hosts Paul and Silas. When the mob cannot find them it drags Jason and some believers before the politarchs, accusing them of saying there is another king, Jesus. Jason posts bond and they are released. Paul says Jason sends greetings from Corinth in Romans 16:21 and calls him a fellow countryman.
A member of the Areopagus council who believes after Paul’s speech. A woman named Damaris and others also believe. Later tradition made him the first bishop of Athens.

A Jewish couple who left Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews. They work with Paul at Corinth, go with him to Ephesus, and explain the way of God more accurately to Apollos. Paul calls them coworkers in Romans 16. In Romans 16 Paul greets “Prisca and Aquila,” who “have risked their lives for me,” and “the church that meets at their house.” They are back in Rome after Claudius’s edict. From Ephesus Paul sends greetings from “Aquila and Prisca,” and “the church that meets at their house” (1 Corinthians 16:19). They had first met him in Corinth. Paul writes, “Greet Prisca and Aquila” (2 Timothy 4:19). They appear to be back in the east, probably at Ephesus. Adolf von Harnack suggested that Priscilla was the writer of Hebrews, and that the name was left out because a woman had written it. The suggestion is old and unproved, and the writer uses a masculine form of a word for himself in 11:32.
rel: Husband and wife

bio: A Jew from Alexandria, ’mighty in the Scriptures,’ who teaches accurately about Jesus though he knows only John’s baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain more. He then helps the believers in Achaia. Paul says, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.” Some Corinthians said “I follow Apollos,” but Paul treats him as a fellow servant and says he “strongly urged him” to visit Corinth again. Paul asks Titus to help “Zenas the lawyer and Apollos” on their way (Titus 3:13). The two are probably passing through Crete. Martin Luther suggested that Apollos wrote Hebrews, since Acts 18:24 calls him an eloquent man who knew the Scriptures well and who came from Alexandria, which fits the style and the use of the Greek Old Testament. The letter does not name its author.

Brother of the philosopher Seneca. He dismisses the Jews’ charge against Paul as a dispute over words and names, and ignores the beating of Sosthenes in front of his court. An inscription at Delphi helps date his term.
rel: Brother of Seneca

bio: A maker of silver shrines of Artemis who rallies fellow craftsmen: Paul’s preaching threatens both their trade and the greatness of the goddess. The crowd fills the theater and shouts for two hours. A different Demetrius, with “a good testimony from everyone,” is commended in 3 John 12. Nothing links the two.

He quiets the crowd by saying that Ephesus is guardian of the temple of Artemis, that the Christians have not robbed temples, and that any complaint should go to the courts. He then dismisses the assembly.
A young man seated in a third-story window while Paul talks until midnight. He falls asleep, falls to the ground and is taken up dead. Paul bends over him and says “his life is in him.”

Paul calls him ’the beloved physician.’ The ’we’ passages in Acts (from Troas to Philippi, and from Philippi to Jerusalem, and in the voyage to Rome) suggest the writer joined Paul at those points. Luke and Aristarchus are with him on the sea voyage. In Colossians 4:14 he is “Luke, the beloved physician.” Paul says, “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings, with Mark, Aristarchus and Demas.

The commander of the garrison at the Fortress of Antonia. He rescues Paul from the mob, learns that he is a Roman citizen, and after hearing of a plot sends him with a strong escort to Felix at Caesarea with a letter.
A young man who hears about the plot of the forty men and tells Paul and the tribune. He is the only member of Paul’s family mentioned in Acts.
rel: Son of Paul’s sister

bio: Antonius Felix, a freed slave who rose to be procurator. He hears Paul’s case, keeps him in custody for two years, and with his wife Drusilla listens to Paul speak about faith, justice and judgment, until he sends Paul away.
rel: Husband of Drusilla

bio: A Jewish princess, daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Bernice. She hears Paul speak with her husband.
rel: Sister of Agrippa II and Bernice

bio: The advocate who accuses Paul before Felix, opening with flattery and calling him a ’plague’ who stirs up riots among all the Jews.
Porcius Festus succeeds Felix. Wanting to please the Jews, he asks if Paul will go up to Jerusalem; Paul appeals to Caesar. Festus consults King Agrippa and sends Paul to Rome.

sub: King of territories east and north of Galilee
bio: Son of Herod Agrippa I, expert in Jewish customs and questions. He hears Paul with his sister Bernice and Festus, and answers, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” He tells Festus that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.
rel: Brother of Bernice and Drusilla

bio: Daughter of Herod Agrippa I. She accompanies her brother to Caesarea “with great pomp” and sits with him as Paul speaks.
rel: Sister of Agrippa II

bio: The Roman officer who takes charge of Paul and other prisoners on the voyage to Italy. He treats Paul kindly, trusts the pilot over Paul, and later stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners so as to save Paul.
The leading Roman official on the island, who welcomes the shipwrecked party for three days. Paul heals his father of fever and dysentery.
A follower of Jesus from the beginning, nominated with Joseph Barsabbas. The believers pray and the lot falls to him, so he is counted with the eleven apostles in place of Judas.

n: The man at the Beautiful Gate
bio: A man over forty, carried each day to the temple to beg. Peter and John take his hand and he walks in the name of Jesus, and enters the temple leaping and praising God.
A man who had never walked. He listens to Paul, who sees that he has faith to be made well and tells him to stand up. The crowd takes it as proof that the gods have come down.

Jews who spoke Greek and often came from the Diaspora. Their widows are overlooked in the daily food, which leads to the choice of the Seven. Persecution after Stephen falls most on them, and they carry the message to Antioch.

Seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom, chosen by the church and set apart by the apostles’ prayer: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus of Antioch. All have Greek names.

About 120 gather in Acts 1, and about three thousand are added at Pentecost. They meet in the temple and in homes, share possessions, and are known as followers of “the Way” before they are called Christians at Antioch. In Romans the believers are those who are justified by faith, not by works of the law. In 1 Corinthians Paul calls them “the saints” and says they “will judge the world.” In 2 Corinthians they are “a letter from Christ” (3:3), “must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (5:10), and are “a new creation” (5:17). In Galatians they are “sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (3:26), “all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28), heirs “according to the promise” (3:29), and called to bear one another’s burdens (6:2). In Ephesians they are chosen “before the foundation of the world” (1:4), saved “by grace” through faith (2:8), “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (2:10), and “fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (2:19). In Colossians believers are “the elect of God, holy and beloved” (3:12), who have been “raised with Christ” (3:1). In 1 Thessalonians believers are those who “believe that Jesus died and rose again” (4:14), and the Thessalonians are told to “encourage one another” with these words (4:18). First Timothy 4:12 tells Timothy to “set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” Titus 3:1 asks Titus to “remind the believers” of their duties, and 3:14 says “our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works.”
Non-Jews who attended synagogue and kept parts of the law but were not full converts. Cornelius is one. Luke notes them often as the first Gentiles to listen to Paul in each city.

The two schools that meet Paul in the marketplace. Epicureans taught that the gods do not interfere in human life; Stoics taught that the universe is ordered by a divine reason. Both call Paul a “babbler” and invite him to explain.

Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in each church with prayer and fasting. The elders of Jerusalem join the apostles at the council, and the elders of Ephesus are told by Paul at Miletus to “care for the church of God.” The Ephesian elders came to Paul at Miletus. He told them, “Be shepherds of the church of God,” and warned that “savage wolves will come in among you” (Acts 20:28-29). Ephesians 4:11-16 describes shepherds and teachers whose work is to equip the saints. In 1 Timothy the elders laid their hands on Timothy (4:14), and “elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching” (5:17). Timothy is not to be “too quick in the laying on of hands” (5:22). Titus 1:5-9 tells Titus to “appoint elders in every town” and lists what an elder must be. In 1:7 the same man is called an overseer. James 5:14 tells the sick person to call “the elders of the church” to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. The Greek word is presbyteroi, and James does not say how many there were or how they were chosen. In 1 Peter 5:1-4 Peter, “a fellow elder,” appeals to the elders to be shepherds of God’s flock “not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness.” He promises that when “the Chief Shepherd appears,” they will receive “the crown of glory that will never fade away.” In 2 John 1 and 3 John 1 the writer calls himself “the elder.”

Paul calls the leaders together on the third day after he arrives. Some are persuaded by what he says from morning to evening, and some do not believe. They tell him they have received no letters about him, but know that this sect is spoken against everywhere. Romans speaks to a church in which Jewish and Gentile believers are learning to live together.

On the Orontes River, the city where believers were first called Christians, where Barnabas and Saul taught for a year, and from which the first journey is launched. Paul reports back here after each journey. In Galatians 2:11-14 Paul opposes Peter here. Some place the Jerusalem meeting of 2:1-10 before this event.

A Roman colony in the highlands of what is now Turkey. Paul preaches in the synagogue, a crowd gathers the next Sabbath, and he and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles before opposition drives them out. If the churches of Galatia were in the south, this Roman colony was among the first Paul reached (Acts 13:14-50). Paul recalls “the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:11).

The ancient city where Saul goes to arrest believers, is healed by Ananias, preaches in the synagogues and escapes in a basket. He later retells the Damascus road story twice. Paul remembers the escape from this city in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33. Paul says he “returned to Damascus” after going to Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

A great trading and university city in south-east Asia Minor. Paul says he was born here and is “a citizen of no obscure city.” Barnabas fetches him from Tarsus to work in Antioch. Paul says he “went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (Galatians 1:21), and Tarsus was the main city of Cilicia.
Herod’s harbor city on the coast, with the governor’s palace. Philip lives here, Cornelius is baptized here, Herod Agrippa dies here, and Paul is tried before Felix, Festus and Agrippa.
The harbor town (modern Jaffa) where Peter raises Tabitha, stays with Simon the tanner, and sees the vision of the sheet before the men from Cornelius arrive.
Barnabas’s home. Paul, Barnabas and Mark cross the island from Salamis to Paphos on the first journey, where Sergius Paulus believes. Later Barnabas and Mark sail there again.

Where Paul heals a lame man, is called Hermes, and is stoned and dragged out as dead. Timothy comes from here, and Paul picks him up on the second journey. Paul’s stoning here (Acts 14:19) is probably what he means by “once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:25). Some read “you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God” (Galatians 4:14) and “the marks of Jesus” (6:17) in the light of what happened here (Acts 14:11-19), if the Galatians were southern. The letter itself does not make the link. Timothy was from Lystra or the area (Acts 16:1-2). First Timothy speaks of “the previous prophecies about you” (1:18) and “the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders” (4:14). The letter does not say where this happened. Timothy’s grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5) belonged to this area, and Paul recalls his sufferings “in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (3:11).

Where Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue and a great number believe, before a plot to stone them sends them to Lystra and Derbe. Paul recalls “the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:11).
The last town on the first journey, where Paul and Barnabas make many disciples. Gaius of Derbe travels with Paul later.

The first city Paul preaches in on European soil. Lydia believes by the river, a slave girl is freed from a spirit, and Paul and Silas are jailed and released by an earthquake. Philippians is addressed to the church here (1:1). Paul says that “in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (4:15). Paul says he had “already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi” before he came to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

Where Paul reasons from the Scriptures in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and a mob forms. Paul writes two letters to the church here. Philippians 4:16 says, “even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again.” First and Second Thessalonians are letters to the church here. The first one says the message of the Lord “ring out from you to Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:8), and the second shows a church still under pressure (2 Thessalonians 1:4). Paul says Demas “has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10).
Where the Jews are “more noble” than those in Thessalonica, receiving the word eagerly and examining the Scriptures every day.

The home of philosophy. Paul argues in the synagogue and the marketplace and speaks to the Areopagus, using an altar to an unknown god, and Greek poets, to introduce the God who raised Jesus. Paul says he was “left on our own in Athens” and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there (1 Thessalonians 3:1-2).

A busy commercial city on a narrow isthmus with two harbors. Paul stays eighteen months, working with Aquila and Priscilla, and writes at least two letters to the church here. Romans was probably written from Corinth, in the home of Gaius, with Tertius as scribe. The Roman colony where Paul founded the church and to which 1 Corinthians is addressed. In 2 Corinthians Paul writes to this church after a painful second visit here, and says he is coming “a third time” (12:14). Most readers think Paul wrote both letters to Thessalonica here, soon after Timothy returned from Macedonia (1 Thessalonians 3:6; Acts 18:5). Paul says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth” (2 Timothy 4:20).

The great port and the center of the worship of Artemis. Paul stays about three years, working in the hall of Tyrannus, and the whole province of Asia hears the word. Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, where he stays “until Pentecost” because “a great door for effective work has opened” (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). Paul’s hardship in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8) may refer to trouble here, though the letter does not say. Ephesians is addressed “to the saints in Ephesus” (1:1), though some oldest copies omit the city’s name. Paul spent about three years here (Acts 20:31), and Timothy was later left in charge (1 Timothy 1:3). Paul spent two or three years here (Acts 19:8-10), and the church at Colossae may have come out of that work, since he writes to them as people he had not met (Colossians 2:1). Some scholars suggest he wrote Colossians from an Ephesian prison. First Timothy is set here: Paul asks Timothy to “stay on at Ephesus” (1:3). The letter seems to place Timothy here. Onesiphorus had “ministered” to Paul “in Ephesus” (1:18), Paul says he has sent Tychicus “to Ephesus” (4:12), and he sends greetings to Prisca and Aquila (4:19). It does not say outright where Timothy is.

Where Paul sees the vision of the man from Macedonia and later raises Eutychus. Paul found an open door here but could not rest because Titus was missing (2 Corinthians 2:12-13). Paul says he left his cloak “with Carpus at Troas” (2 Timothy 4:13).

Where Paul gives his farewell to the elders of Ephesus, and kneels with them on the beach to pray. The elders of Ephesus met Paul at Miletus (Acts 20:17-38). He told them, “Be shepherds of the church of God” (Acts 20:28), and Ephesians 4:11 lists “pastors and teachers” among Christ’s gifts. Paul says, “Trophimus I left sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20).
Called Melite in Acts. The wrecked ship’s company comes ashore in a bay, and Paul is bitten by a viper, heals the father of Publius, and stays three months.

The ship’s course runs under Crete. Paul advises wintering at Fair Havens, and the ship is driven off by the storm. Paul says he left Titus “in Crete” (Titus 1:5), and quotes a Cretan poet (1:12). The letter does not name any town on the island.

The goal of the book. Paul has been told “you must bear witness also in Rome.” He lives there under guard in his own rented house for two years, welcoming all who come. Romans is Paul’s letter to the church in the capital, which he plans to visit on his way to Spain. If Ephesians was written from Rome, Paul wrote “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1) and “an ambassador in chains” (6:20) while under guard here (Acts 28:16, 30). If Philippians was written from Rome, Paul’s chains had become known “throughout the whole palace guard” (1:13), and “the household of Caesar” sent greetings (4:22). If Colossians was written from Rome, Paul was “in chains” here (4:3, 18) with Aristarchus, Mark, Luke and others (4:10-14). In 2 Timothy Paul is a prisoner here. Onesiphorus “searched diligently until he found me” (1:17), Paul is “chained like a criminal” (2:9), and he expects his “departure” (4:6). Friends there send greetings (4:21). Revelation never names Rome. Most readers find it behind “Babylon the great,” the woman who sits on seven mountains and is “the great city that rules over the kings of the earth” (17:18).

The region of northern Greece that includes Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul crosses to it after his vision at Troas. Macedonia gave to the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). Paul plans to come to Corinth after going through Macedonia (1 Corinthians 16:5). In 2 Corinthians Paul goes on here from Troas and meets Titus (2:13; 7:5). The churches give “according to their ability and even beyond it” out of deep poverty (8:1-5), and “the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs” (11:9). Philippians 4:15 speaks of the time “when I left Macedonia,” when the church at Philippi alone partnered with Paul in giving and receiving. The Thessalonians became “an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7), and they showed love “to all the brothers throughout Macedonia” (4:10). Paul says he urged Timothy to stay at Ephesus “on my departure to Macedonia” (1 Timothy 1:3).

Southern Greece, with Athens and Corinth. Gallio is proconsul here. Achaia gave with Macedonia to the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). The Roman province whose capital was Corinth. Paul calls the household of Stephanas its first converts (1 Corinthians 16:15). Paul addresses 2 Corinthians to “all the saints throughout Achaia” (1:1) and says his boasting “will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia” (11:10). The Thessalonians became “an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7).

The western part of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its main city. Paul is forbidden by the Spirit to preach in Asia on the second journey, then stays there about three years on the third. The province whose churches send greetings in 1 Corinthians 16:19. In 2 Corinthians 1:8 Paul tells the church of hardships “in the province of Asia” that left him despairing “even of life.” The Roman province whose capital was Ephesus. Because some of the oldest copies of Ephesians leave out “in Ephesus,” some scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. Paul says, “everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes” (2 Timothy 1:15).

sub: Servant of the church in Cenchrea
bio: A woman whom Paul commends at the end of Romans as “our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea.” He asks the Romans to “welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints” and to help her with anything she needs, because she “has been a great help to many people, including me.” Many scholars think she carried the letter to Rome.
rel: Fellow worker of Paul, from the harbor town of Corinth

bio: Paul spoke the letter and Tertius wrote it down. Near the end he adds his own greeting: “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.” It is the one place where a scribe of Paul’s letters names himself.

“Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church,” sends greetings from Corinth. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 1:14 that he baptized a Gaius there, and many think it is the same man. Gaius was a very common name, and Acts 19:29 and 20:4 mention other men called Gaius. Paul says he baptized Gaius (1 Corinthians 1:14). 3 John is written to another “beloved Gaius” (3 John 1). Nothing shows he is the same man, though Bede in the 8th century thought so.

Paul sends greetings from “Erastus, the city treasurer.” A man of that name appears in Acts 19:22 as one of Paul’s helpers and in 2 Timothy 4:20 as staying in Corinth. A paving stone near the Corinth theater records an Erastus who paid for the pavement in return for his office. Paul says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth” (2 Timothy 4:20).
rel: Believer with a public post in Corinth

bio: Paul greets “Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners.” He says “they are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was.” Early writers took Junia to be a woman, and many scholars think the pair were a couple. Paul does not say where or when he was imprisoned with them.
rel: Jewish believers, probably from before Paul’s own conversion

bio: Paul greets “my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.” Since the letter greets him in Rome, he had moved there. The note shows how freely Christians traveled across the empire.

Paul greets “Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.” Mark 15:21 names Rufus and Alexander as the sons of Simon of Cyrene, and some think this is the same Rufus because Mark was probably written for Rome. That cannot be proved, since Rufus was a common name.
rel: Possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene

bio: In Romans 5 Paul sets Adam beside Christ: “just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin,” so the free gift of grace comes through one man, Jesus Christ. Paul says death reigned “from Adam until Moses,” even over those who had not broken a command as Adam did. Paul says “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive,” and calls Christ “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22, 45). In 1 Timothy Paul says “Adam was formed first, and then Eve,” and “it was not Adam who was deceived” (2:13-14). Jude 14 counts the generations from him: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam.”
rel: Father of the human family

bio: Romans 4 mentions “the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb” along with the age of Abraham’s body, and says that Abraham did not waver in unbelief about God’s promise. In Romans 9:9 Paul recalls the promise “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” In Galatians 4 she is the “free woman” whose child was born “through the promise” (4:22-23), and Paul says “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (4:26). Hebrews 11:11 says that Sarah, though barren and past the age, received power to conceive because she considered the one who promised to be faithful. In 1 Peter 3:6 she is held up to Christian wives because she “obeyed Abraham and called him lord.” Peter says that the readers are “her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.”
rel: Wife of Abraham, mother of Isaac

bio: In Romans 9 Paul recalls that God’s promise came through Isaac, “not the children of the flesh,” and then through Jacob rather than his twin Esau, before either was born. Paul quotes Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” He uses them to show that God’s purpose rests on his call and not on human descent. Hebrews 11:9 says that Abraham lived in tents, “as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise.” Isaac and Jacob blessed their sons by faith (11:20-21), and 12:16-17 warns against Esau, who “for a single meal sold his birthright” and later “could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.”
rel: Son and grandson of Abraham

sub: The king of Egypt in the Exodus
bio: Paul quotes God’s word to Pharaoh from Exodus 9:16: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” Romans 9 uses him as an example of God’s sovereign choice in showing mercy or letting hearts harden.
rel: Ruler of Egypt in the time of Moses

bio: Paul addresses “all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints,” a group he has not yet met. The church probably met in several households and began with Jews and converts to Judaism, then grew among Gentiles. Paul says “your faith is being proclaimed all over the world” (1:8) and later greets many of them by name.

Paul speaks to a Jewish reader who relies on the law and boasts in God (2:17), and asks what advantage the Jew has (3:1). In chapters 9-11 he grieves over Israel’s unbelief, insists that God has not rejected his people, and says “all Israel will be saved” (11:26).

In Romans 1 Paul describes the Gentile world that turned from God to idols. In Romans 15 he says Christ became “a servant of the circumcised” so that “the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy,” and describes himself as “a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles.”
Paul warns the Gentile believers in Rome not to boast over the Jewish branches that were broken off, because “You do not support the root, but the root supports you” (11:18).

In Romans 14-15 some believers eat anything and others eat only vegetables, and some keep certain days and others treat all days alike. Paul tells both sides to welcome each other: “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.” In 1 Corinthians 8 the “strong” know an idol is nothing, and the “weak” are still accustomed to idols and have a weak conscience.
Paul says that “at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace” (11:5), as in Elijah’s day when God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal.

Paul tells the believers in Rome to “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities” (13:1), to pay taxes and revenue, and to give respect and honor to those who are owed them. Romans was written in the early years of Nero’s rule. Titus 3:1 tells Titus to remind believers “to submit to rulers and authorities.”
Quoting Isaiah 52:7, Paul asks, “And how can they preach unless they are sent?” and says “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.”
Timothy, Lucius, Jason and Sosipater send greetings to Rome, along with Quartus, Gaius and Erastus. Paul calls Lucius, Jason and Sosipater “my fellow countrymen,” which probably means fellow Jews.

Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, Epenetus, Mary, Andronicus and Junia, Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, Herodion, Tryphena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and Olympas, along with the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus. Many of the names were common among slaves and freed people.

The port on the Saronic Gulf, about eight miles from Corinth. Phoebe was a servant of the church there (Romans 16:1), and Acts 18:18 says Paul shaved his head at Cenchrea because of a vow before sailing for Syria.

The region across the sea from Italy, later organized as Dalmatia. Paul says that “from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum” he has fully proclaimed the gospel (Romans 15:19). Acts does not mention it.

sub: The western end of the empire
bio: Paul hoped to visit Rome and then go on to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28). The New Testament does not say whether he got there, though 1 Clement says he reached “the limit of the west.”

sub: Her household told Paul of the quarrels
bio: Paul writes, “My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you.” Nothing else is known about her. The wording suggests she was a woman of some means whose household members, perhaps slaves or freed people, traveled between Corinth and Ephesus.
rel: Believer known to Paul and the Corinthians

bio: Paul says, “I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius.” Acts 18:8 calls Crispus the ruler of the synagogue, who believed “together with his entire household.” Many think this Gaius is the host of Romans 16:23, since Gaius was a very common name.
rel: Early converts at Corinth

bio: Paul opens the letter “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes.” Acts 18:17 names a Sosthenes as the synagogue ruler who was beaten in front of Gallio, and he may be the same man, though the name was not rare.

Paul baptized “the household of Stephanas” (1:16) and says “Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints” (16:15).
