He urges the church “to submit to such as these,” and is glad that Stephanas, with Fortunatus and Achaicus, has come to him.
rel: Leader among the Corinthian believers

sub: Visitors who came to Paul at Ephesus
bio: Paul writes, “I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well.” Nothing more is known of them. Fortunatus is a Latin name and Achaicus means “from Achaia.”

sub: Those who crucified the Lord of glory
bio: Paul says, “None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Some take the “rulers” as the human officials who put Jesus to death, others also include the unseen powers behind them.

sub: A member living with his father’s wife
bio: Paul has heard that “A man has his father’s wife,” and he tells the church to remove the man: “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.” His name is not given. Scholars disagree whether he is the same person whom Paul asks them to forgive in 2 Corinthians 2:5-8.

Paul writes “To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy.” Most were Gentiles who had worshiped idols (12:2), with some Jews (Acts 18:4-8), and a mix of rich and poor. They were gifted, divided, proud, and loved by Paul, who calls them “my beloved children” (4:14). In 2 Corinthians Paul calls them “our letter, inscribed on our hearts” (3:2), says “Our hearts are open wide” (6:11), asks them to finish their gift for Jerusalem (chapters 8-9), and grieves over the quarreling and sin that remain (12:20-21).
rel: Church that Paul founded about AD 50

sub: The church as one body with many parts
bio: Paul writes, “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.” He also says “your bodies are members of Christ” (6:15). The body is made up of Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, with different gifts, and “if one part suffers, every part suffers with it.” In Ephesians the church is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (1:23), the “one body” in which Jews and Gentiles are reconciled (2:16), and the body that “grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part” (4:16). Christ is “the head of the church, His body” (5:23). In Colossians Christ “is the head of the body, the church” (1:18). The body “supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow” (2:19), and believers are “called as members of one body” (3:15).

In chapter 7 Paul says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, and that the husband and wife owe each other their duty. He tells the married, “(not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband,” and gives his own view on mixed marriages with an unbelieving partner.

Paul says “It is good to abstain from sexual relations,” that he wishes all were as he is, and that those who cannot control themselves should marry. He advises the unmarried and widows to remain as they are “because of the present crisis.”

Paul tells slaves, “Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.” He adds that “he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman,” and that “he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave.”
Paul writes, “in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize.” He applies the picture to himself: “I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air.”

sub: Apostles who took their wives along
bio: Paul asks, “Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas?” Peter (Cephas) and the brothers of Jesus were known to the Corinthians, and the passage suggests they traveled with their wives.

Paul says that “our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea.” Yet most of them fell: “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come.” Hebrews 3:7-4:13 draws a warning from Israel’s time in the wilderness: the generation that heard God’s voice hardened their hearts at Kadesh and did not enter his rest, and the readers are told not to follow their example of unbelief. Jude 5 uses the same warning: after the people were brought out of Egypt, “He destroyed those who did not believe.”

n: The rich and the poor in Corinth
sub: Those who ate at the Lord’s Supper
bio: Paul says that each one “goes ahead without sharing his meal” at the Lord’s Supper: “While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.” He asks those with homes to eat there, and says some “humiliate those who have nothing.”

sub: Those who speak for God in the church
bio: Paul ranks prophets second after apostles (12:28) and says “he who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” He wants prophets to speak in turn, and their words to be weighed.

Paul does not forbid speaking in tongues, and says “I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy.” He wants tongues to be interpreted, so that the whole church can understand, and says “in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.”

Paul pictures “some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers” coming into the meeting and asks what they would think if everyone spoke in tongues: “will they not say that you are out of your minds?” Prophecy instead convicts the outsider and leads him to worship.

In the creed Paul lists those to whom the risen Christ appeared: “He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve,” “more than five hundred brothers at once,” then James, “all the apostles,” and “last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth.”
The sanctuary of Poseidon about ten miles east of Corinth, where the games were held every two years. Paul draws his picture of racing and discipline from the athletes there (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

sub: Churches Paul organized the collection in
bio: The central highlands of what is now Turkey. Paul tells the Corinthians to do as he “directed the churches of Galatia” about the collection for the saints (1 Corinthians 16:1). Acts 18:23 says he strengthened the disciples there. Paul addresses his letter to “the churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2). Some scholars place them in the north, near Ankara; others in the Roman province’s southern cities where Acts 13-14 shows Paul preaching. Paul says, “Crescens has gone to Galatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Some early manuscripts read “Gaul.”

The mountain where God met Israel after the exodus. Paul recalls the people there “sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry” (1 Corinthians 10:7, quoting Exodus 32:6). The exact location is uncertain; Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site. Moses came down from the mountain with a shining face, and Paul uses the veil he wore as a picture in 2 Corinthians 3:7-18. Paul says “Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25).

A Greek believer who works with Paul. Galatians 2:1-3 says he went up to Jerusalem with Paul and was not made to be circumcised. In 2 Corinthians Paul waits anxiously for him at Troas, is comforted when he arrives in Macedonia with good news, and sends him back to Corinth to finish the collection. Many think he carried the sharp letter. Paul calls him “my partner and fellow worker among you” (8:23). Acts never names him. Paul took him to Jerusalem, and “not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek” (Galatians 2:3). Paul says, “Titus to Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Paul addresses him as “my true child in our common faith” (Titus 1:4) and says he left him on Crete to “appoint elders in every town” (1:5). He tells him to “speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine” (2:1), says “Let no one despise you” (2:15), and asks him to come to Nicopolis once Artemas or Tychicus arrives (3:12).
rel: Gentile coworker of Paul

bio: Paul writes, “if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you.” The majority had punished him, and Paul asks them to “forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (2:5-8). In 7:12 he speaks of “the one who did wrong” and “the one who was harmed.” The man is not named, and scholars still disagree whether he is the man of 1 Corinthians 5 or someone who insulted Paul during the painful visit.

Paul quotes what they say: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account” (10:10). They look at “outward appearances” and “compare themselves with themselves” (10:7, 12). Paul answers that he will be the same in person as in his letters. He does not say whether they are the same people as the “super-apostles.”

Visitors who came to Corinth boasting of their credentials and preaching “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.” Paul calls them “false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ,” and says he is “in no way inferior to those ’super-apostles’” (11:5, 13; 12:11). They claimed to be Hebrews, Israelites and descendants of Abraham (11:22), and the church put up with anyone who “enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you” (11:20). Paul does not name them, and scholars still debate who they were.

sub: Poor churches that gave beyond their means
bio: The churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul holds them up as an example: “In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity” (8:2). They “gave according to their ability and even beyond it,” and Paul had boasted to them of the Corinthians’ eagerness (9:2). Some Macedonians were to come with Paul to Corinth (9:4).

Titus is sent ahead with two brothers Paul does not name. One is “praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel” and was “chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering” (8:18-19). The other has an “earnestness” that “has been proven many times and in many ways” (8:22). Paul calls them “messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ” (8:23). Acts 20:4 names seven men who later went with the gift.

sub: How Paul asks the Corinthians to give
bio: Paul pictures giving as sowing: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.” Each one gives “what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (9:6-7). God “supplies seed to the sower and bread for food” (9:10), and Paul ends, “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”

sub: The poor believers the gift was for
bio: The believers in Jerusalem, many of them poor, for whom the collection is taken. Paul calls it “this service to the saints” (8:4) and says it overflows in “many expressions of thanksgiving to God” (9:12). Their prayers for the Corinthians will “express their affection for you” (9:14). Romans 15:25-27 says Macedonia and Achaia both gave.

Paul says the gospel is veiled to “those who are perishing,” because “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (4:3-4). He then tells the believers, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers,” and asks what a believer has “in common with an unbeliever” (6:14-15).

Paul writes, “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (11:3). The story is in Genesis 3, and Adam named her Eve because she would be “the mother of all the living” (Genesis 3:20). In 1 Timothy 2:13-14 Paul refers to Eve in giving reasons for his instruction about teaching, and writes that “the woman who was deceived” fell into transgression. How this argument applies is debated.
rel: First woman, wife of Adam

bio: Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom from Petra for about forty-eight years, from about 9 BC to AD 40. Paul says that in Damascus “the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me” (2 Corinthians 11:32). How an official of Aretas came to hold power in Damascus is debated.

Paul writes “to the churches of Galatia” (1:2) and is “amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ” (1:6). He calls them “foolish Galatians” (3:1), reminds them that they received the Spirit by hearing with faith (3:2), and recalls how they once welcomed him “as if I were an angel of God” (4:14). Scholars disagree whether they lived in the old Celtic north of the region or in the southern cities of the Roman province.
rel: Gentile believers in Galatia

bio: Paul says “some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ” (1:7). They press the Gentile believers to be circumcised (6:12), and Paul says they want to “make a good impression outwardly” and “avoid persecution for the cross of Christ.” He says they are “zealous for you, but not in a good way,” because they “want to isolate you from us” (4:17). Their names are not given, and scholars reconstruct their message only from what Paul says against it.

sub: Those who spied on freedom in Jerusalem
bio: Paul says “some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us” (2:4). He says, “We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you” (2:5). Some link them to the teachers who came to Galatia, but the letter does not say so.

Paul calls “James, Cephas, and John” those “reputed to be pillars” (2:9). He reports that they added nothing to his message, recognized the grace given to him, and gave him and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship,” agreeing that Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised (2:6-9).
rel: Leaders of the Jerusalem church

sub: Those whose arrival changed Peter’s table
bio: Paul says that before “certain men came from James,” Peter ate with the Gentiles, but “when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group” (2:12). The letter does not say what message they carried or whether James sent them to say it.

sub: Sarah’s slave and mother of Ishmael
bio: Abraham’s wife Sarah gave her slave Hagar to Abraham, and she bore Ishmael (Genesis 16). Paul reads the story as a picture: “One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar” (Galatians 4:24). He then says she “corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children” (4:25).
rel: Slave of Sarah, mother of Ishmael

bio: Paul writes, “if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (6:1). The word describes believers who live by the Spirit, as in 5:25, not a special class.

sub: Paul’s word for life without the Spirit
bio: In Galatians “flesh” often means human nature on its own, as opposed to the Spirit. Paul says “the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh” (5:17), lists “the acts of the flesh” (5:19-21), and says “those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (5:24).

Paul asks, “Why then was the law given?” and answers that “it was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed” (3:19). He says it was “our guardian to lead us to Christ” (3:24), that it cannot give life (3:21), and that Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law” (3:13). He also says the whole law is fulfilled in one command: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (5:14).

sub: The Nabatean lands east and south of Judea
bio: Paul says that after his call he “went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus” (1:17). In his day Arabia usually meant the Nabatean kingdom, whose capital was Petra. The letter does not say where he stayed or what he did, and he also says Hagar stands for “Mount Sinai in Arabia” (4:25).

Paul writes “To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus” (1:1). Some of the oldest copies leave out “in Ephesus,” so the letter may have been meant for several churches in Asia. Paul says he has “heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints” (1:15). Most of them were Gentiles who had once lived “fulfilling the cravings of our flesh” (2:3) and “without hope and without God in the world” (2:12). Paul had spent about three years in the city (Acts 20:31).
rel: Mostly Gentile believers in Asia

bio: Paul calls him “the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord” and says, “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts” (6:21-22). Acts 20:4 names him as a man of Asia who traveled with Paul. He also carries the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9) and is later sent to Crete or Ephesus (Titus 3:12; 2 Timothy 4:12). Colossians 4:7-8 gives his job: “Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord.” Paul sends him “that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.” Paul says, “Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus” (2 Timothy 4:12). Paul says he will send “Artemas or Tychicus” to Titus (3:12), probably to take his place on Crete. The letter does not say which of them came.
rel: Paul’s messenger from Asia

sub: The slave who returned with Tychicus
bio: Ephesians does not name him. Colossians 4:9 says, “With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.” Paul’s letter to Philemon asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). He is a living example of what Ephesians 6:5-9 says about slaves and masters. Paul calls him “our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you” (4:9) and sends him with Tychicus. Philemon 10-16 tells why he was away. In Philemon he is the slave for whom Paul appeals: “my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains” (verse 10). Paul says, “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me” (verse 11), and plays on the meaning of his name, “useful.” He is to be received “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (verse 16). The letter does not say how he came to Paul or whether Philemon set him free. Ignatius names a bishop of Ephesus Onesimus about AD 110, but a link to this man is only a guess.
rel: Slave, later a brother in Christ

sub: The unseen forces Ephesians speaks of
bio: Paul says Christ is seated “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion” (1:21), and God’s wisdom is made known “to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms” through the church (3:10). He also says “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (6:12). The letter gives no names and no lists. Colossians names “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities” among the things created in Christ (1:16). Christ is “the head over every ruler and authority” (2:10), and on the cross He disarmed “the powers and authorities” (2:15).

Paul tells Gentile readers to remember that they were “separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world” (2:12). Now they are “no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (2:19), and “fellow heirs” (3:6). He also tells them that they “must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking” (4:17).

sub: The nearer ones and the first to hope
bio: Paul speaks of those “called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision” (2:11), of “the commonwealth of Israel” (2:12), and of “we, who were the first to hope in Christ” (1:12), meaning Jewish believers. He says Christ “has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14), and that the Gentiles are “fellow heirs” with them (3:6).

sub: The life put on in Christ
bio: Paul tells his readers “to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires,” and “to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (4:22-24). He then spells out what that looks like: truth, honest anger, honest work, gracious speech, kindness and forgiveness (4:25-32).

sub: Called to love as Christ loved
bio: Paul writes, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (5:25). He says husbands “ought to love their wives as their own bodies” (5:28) and that “each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself” (5:33). The command to submit that comes first (5:21) is addressed to everyone, and the weight in this section falls on the husband’s costly love.

Paul writes, “Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord” (5:22), after saying all believers should “submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21). He compares the husband’s headship to Christ’s as head of the church (5:23) and ends, “the wife must respect her husband” (5:33). Scholars disagree about how far the instruction reaches today.

sub: The household’s young and the head
bio: Paul tells children, “Obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (6:1), and quotes the commandment “Honor your father and mother” with its promise (6:2-3). He tells fathers, “do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (6:4).

sub: The most unequal pair in the household
bio: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters “with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ” (6:5), as “servants of Christ” (6:6). He tells masters to “do the same for your slaves” and to “give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him” (6:9). Some Christian readers have used the passage to defend slavery, and others to show that its foundation was undone. Colossians gives the same pair in a short form: “Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything” (3:22), and “Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1).

sub: The foundation of the household of God
bio: Paul says God’s household is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” (2:20). He says the mystery of Christ “has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets” (3:5). In 4:11 apostles and prophets are listed among Christ’s gifts to the church. Scholars disagree whether the prophets are New Testament or Old Testament figures. Jude 17 tells its readers to “remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

sub: Apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers
bio: Paul quotes Psalm 68 and says that when Christ ascended he “gave gifts to men” (4:8). He lists them: “it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ” (4:11-12). The goal is that “we all reach unity in the faith” and “grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head” (4:13-15).

sub: A wealthy city in the Lycus Valley
bio: Paul does not mention Laodicea in Ephesians, but Colossians 4:16 speaks of “the letter from Laodicea,” which some scholars have connected to this one. Tychicus carries both letters. Revelation 3:14-22 later addresses the church here. Paul says he is struggling for “those at Laodicea” (2:1), greets “the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha” (4:15), and asks that Colossians be read there and that the Colossians read “the letter from Laodicea” (4:16).

sub: A smaller town up the Lycus Valley
bio: Onesimus and Tychicus travel to Colossae (Colossians 4:7-9), the same trip on which Tychicus carries Ephesians (6:21-22). The town was once a center of the wool trade but had fallen behind its neighbors Laodicea and Hierapolis by Paul’s day. Colossians is addressed to the church here (1:2). Epaphras, Onesimus and Archippus are from this town or its neighborhood (4:9, 12, 17). Philemon is usually placed at Colossae, since Archippus (Philemon 2) and Onesimus (Colossians 4:9, 17) belong to that church.

Paul writes “To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). Their “partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (1:5) shows in the gift they sent him by Epaphroditus (4:18). Acts 16 begins the church with Lydia and the jailer and their households. Paul says they are “encountering the same struggle you saw I had” (1:30), tells them to “shine as lights in the world” (2:15), and calls them “my joy and crown” (4:1). He also hears of a quarrel between two women (4:2).
rel: A Roman colony’s church

sub: The leaders Paul greets by title
bio: The greeting reads “together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). No names are given and no duties are listed. This is the only one of Paul’s letters whose opening mentions these two groups. First Timothy 3:1-13 lists what is needed in an overseer (“above reproach, the husband of but one wife,” “able to teach”) and in deacons (“dignified, not double-tongued”). Whether the overseer and the elders are the same office is debated.
rel: Leaders of the church at Philippi

sub: Those who heard that Paul was in chains for Christ
bio: Paul writes, “it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ” (1:13). The Greek word (praitorion) can mean the emperor’s guard, a governor’s headquarters, or the staff of a palace, and scholars disagree about which Paul means. Acts 28:16 says that in Rome he was allowed to live with a soldier guarding him.
rel: Soldiers and staff around Paul

sub: Rivals who preach Christ from bad motives
bio: Paul writes, “some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill” (1:15). The former “preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains” (1:17). Paul says, “in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice” (1:18). He does not name them.
al: Some preach Christ out of envy

sub: People Paul warns the church to watch out for
bio: Paul writes, “Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh!” (3:2). He contrasts them with “we who are the circumcision,” who “worship by the Spirit of God” and “put no confidence in the flesh” (3:3). The letter does not name them. Many scholars think they were teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised.

sub: Those whose minds are set on earthly things
bio: Paul says, with tears, “Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things” (3:18-19). He sets them against those whose “citizenship is in heaven” (3:20). The letter does not name them, and scholars disagree about whether they are the same people as in 3:2.
al: Enemies of the cross of Christ

bio: Paul calls him “my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs” (2:25). He fell “sick indeed, nearly unto death” (2:27), and he was distressed that the Philippians had heard of it (2:26). Paul sends him back, so that they may “welcome him in the Lord with great joy,” because he nearly died “risking his life” (2:29-30). He brought the church’s gifts (4:18). The name was common, and Epaphras in Colossians 1:7 is probably a different man.
rel: A man of Philippi

sub: Two women who worked beside Paul
bio: Paul writes, “I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord” (4:2). He asks his “true yokefellow” to “help these women who have labored with me for the gospel” (4:3). Nothing else is known about them. Acts 16:13-15 tells of women who gathered to pray at Philippi.

sub: A fellow worker named in the letter
bio: Paul names him among “the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life” (4:3). Nothing else is said about him. Some later writers thought he was Clement of Rome, but the name was very common. Eusebius says that some in the early church, according to Origen, named Clement of Rome as the writer of Hebrews, and Clement’s own letter to the Corinthians draws on Hebrews at length. That shows that Hebrews was known in Rome by the end of the 1st century, though it does not show who wrote it.
rel: Co-worker at Philippi

sub: The person asked to help Euodia and Syntyche
bio: Paul writes, “I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women” (4:3). The Greek word (syzygos) could be a title or a name, and some have wondered whether it was a man named Syzygus. The letter does not say who is meant.
rel: A partner in the work

sub: The emperor’s slaves and freed people
bio: Paul ends, “All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar” (4:22). The phrase meant the emperor’s staff of slaves and freed people, not his family. They worked in Rome and in cities across the empire.

Paul writes “To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae” (1:2). He has “heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints” (1:4), and he delights in their “orderly condition and firm faith in Christ” (2:5). He has not met them (2:1). They learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7), and he warns them against being “taken captive” by teaching that adds rules and powers to Christ (2:8). Several of them were slaves, and at least one house church met in the valley (4:15).
rel: A small church in the Lycus Valley

sub: The Colossian who brought the gospel and the news
bio: Paul calls him “our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf” (1:7). The Colossians “learned it from Epaphras” (1:7), and he told Paul of their “love in the Spirit” (1:8). He “is one of you” (4:12). Paul says he is “always wrestling in prayer for you” (4:12) and “goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis” (4:13). Philemon 23 calls him Paul’s fellow prisoner. The name may be a short form of Epaphroditus, but most scholars think the man of Philippians 2:25 is someone else. Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus” and says he sends greetings (Philemon 23). The word is the one used of Aristarchus in Colossians 4:10.
rel: Founder and pastor of the church at Colossae

sub: Those who offered a “philosophy” in addition to Christ
bio: Paul writes, “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ” (2:8). He mentions rules about “what you eat or drink,” feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths (2:16), “false humility and the worship of angels” (2:18), and slogans such as “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” (2:21). The letter never names them or says how many there were, and scholars still debate whether they were Jewish, pagan, or a mixture.

n: The old self and the new self
sub: Paul’s picture of the life the Colossians left behind and the life they have put on
bio: Paul says, “you have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (3:9-10). The old self shows itself in “sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed” (3:5) and in “anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language” (3:8). The new self wears “compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (3:12), with love as “the bond of perfect unity” (3:14). In this life, “Christ is all and is in all” (3:11).

Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner” (4:10). Acts names him as a Macedonian from Thessalonica who was seized in the riot at Ephesus (19:29), who traveled with Paul (20:4), and who sailed with him to Rome (27:2). Philemon 24 also lists him among Paul’s fellow workers. Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings.
rel: Companion from Thessalonica

sub: A Jewish co-worker with a Roman second name
bio: Paul writes, “Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings” (4:11). He, Aristarchus and Mark are “the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God,” and Paul says “they have been a comfort to me” (4:11). Nothing else is known of him. Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, and Justus was a common Roman name.
rel: A Jewish co-worker with Paul

bio: Paul lists him with Luke: “Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas send you greetings” (4:14). Philemon 24 names him as a fellow worker. In 2 Timothy 4:10 Paul says that Demas has deserted him because he loved the present world. Paul says, “Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10). Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings. He is not called a fellow prisoner.
rel: Companion of Paul in prison

sub: A woman of Laodicea who hosted a church
bio: Paul writes, “Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house” (4:15). Some manuscripts read “his” or “their” house, and the name could be read as Nymphas, a man, but many editors prefer Nympha and “her house.” Nothing else is known of her. She is one of several women named as hosts of house churches in the New Testament (Acts 12:12; 16:15; Romans 16:3-5).
rel: Host of a house church at Laodicea

sub: A man told to finish his ministry
bio: Paul tells the church to say to Archippus that he should “complete the ministry you have received in the Lord” (4:17). The letter does not say what the ministry was. Philemon 2 calls him “our fellow soldier.” Because Philemon and Colossians were sent together, many suppose he lived in or near Colossae and belonged to Philemon’s circle. Paul calls him “our fellow soldier” and greets him with Philemon and Apphia (Philemon 2). Colossians 4:17 tells him to complete the ministry he received. Some suggest he was Philemon’s son, but the letters do not say.
rel: A minister at Colossae

sub: A hot-spring city across the river from Laodicea
bio: Colossians 4:13 is the only verse in the New Testament that names the city. Paul says that Epaphras “goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.” The city lay on a ridge above the Lycus, known for its hot springs, its cloth and its dyers. Later Christian tradition says the apostle Philip died there.

sub: The church Paul writes to twice
bio: Paul writes “To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:1). Most had “turned to God from idols” (1:9). They welcomed the message “in spite of your great suffering” (1:6), and their faith became known across Macedonia and Achaia (1:7-8). Acts 17:4 says Jews, God-fearing Greeks and leading women joined Paul. Paul had to leave them soon, and he writes to answer their questions about those who have died, the Day of the Lord and those who would not work.
rel: A young church in the capital of Macedonia

sub: The three who send both letters
bio: Both letters open with the same three names: “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy” (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul, Silas and Timothy had all been in Thessalonica (Acts 17:1-10) and Paul says “we” through the letters. Paul writes “I, Paul” in a few places (1 Thessalonians 2:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).
rel: Paul and two coworkers

sub: Believers who had died, and the church’s grief for them
bio: Paul writes, “we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He says that “the dead in Christ will be the first to rise” (4:16) and that “we will always be with the Lord” (4:17). “Sleep” was a common way to speak of death, and Paul uses it for believers who have died. He adds, “whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (5:10).
rel: Believers who had died

sub: The workers Paul asks the church to respect
bio: Paul writes, “we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction” and tells them to “hold them in highest regard because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). They are not named and no office is given. Paul calls them to “live in peace with one another” (5:13).
rel: The unnamed leaders of a young church

bio: Paul tells the church “to admonish the unruly” (1 Thessalonians 5:14) and to “work with your own hands, as we instructed you” (4:11). In the second letter he commands them to “keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life” (2 Thessalonians 3:6) and says, “we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies” (3:11). He asks them to “begin working quietly to earn their own living” (3:12). He does not say why they had stopped, and some think they expected the Lord to come very soon.
rel: Some of the church who would not work

sub: The opponents behind the pressure on the church
bio: Paul says the church suffered “from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews” (1 Thessalonians 2:14). In the second letter he says that “it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) and that they endure “all the persecution and affliction” (1:4). The letters do not name the persecutors, and they give no details of what was done.
rel: The unnamed opponents of the church

sub: A figure Paul says will be revealed before the Day
bio: Paul writes that “the Day of the Lord” will not come “until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). He “will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship” and “seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2:4). The Lord Jesus “will slay” him “with the breath of His mouth and annihilate” him “by the majesty of His arrival” (2:8). Readers disagree on whether this is one person, a series of rulers or a power in history.
rel: An opponent of God in the last days

sub: What holds back the lawless one for now
bio: Paul writes, “you know what is now restraining him, so that he may be revealed at the proper time” (2 Thessalonians 2:6), and “the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way” (2:7). The Thessalonians knew what Paul meant because he had told them (2:5), and the letter does not repeat it. Suggestions include the Roman order, the preaching of the gospel and an angel, and none is certain.
rel: Something or someone that holds back the lawless one

sub: The members of the church who were doing what Paul asked
bio: Paul says, “we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command” (2 Thessalonians 3:4), and tells them, “do not grow weary in well-doing” (3:13). He sets them apart from the idle but asks that even the disobedient be treated “as a brother” (3:15).
rel: The part of the church that kept faith and work

sub: The one Paul says came to save sinners
bio: The letter names him “Christ Jesus” and “our Lord Jesus Christ.” Paul says “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (1 Timothy 1:15), and that there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all” (2:5-6). He is the one “who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate” (6:13), and the hymn in 3:16 says “He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.” In 2 Timothy he is the one who “has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (1:10), who is “raised from the dead, descended from David” (2:8), and who “will judge the living and the dead” (4:1). In Titus he is “Christ Jesus our Savior” (1:4) and “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13), a phrase many read as calling Jesus God. He “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (2:14). In 1 Peter he is the “living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight” (2:4), the one who “committed no sin” (2:22), who “bore our sins in His body on the tree” (2:24), who “suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (3:18), and the “Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25). He is also the “Chief Shepherd” who will appear (5:4). The readers are to “sanctify Christ as Lord” in their hearts (3:15). In 2 Peter he is “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1) and “our Lord and Savior” (3:2, 18), and the writer speaks of his “power and coming” (1:16) and the Day of the Lord (3:10). In 1 John he is “the Word of life” (1:1), “His Son, Jesus Christ” (1:3), “the Righteous One” (2:1), “the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (2:2; 4:10), and the one who “came by water and blood” (5:6). The letter says “Whoever has the Son has life” (5:12) and “He is the true God and eternal life” (5:20). In 2 John he is “Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father” (1:3), and the letter warns against those “refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (1:7). 3 John never uses the names Jesus or Christ. It speaks of him only as “the Name,” for whose sake the brothers went out (3 John 7). In Jude he is “our only Master and Lord” (Jude 4). The readers are “kept in Jesus Christ” (Jude 1) and wait for his mercy “to bring you eternal life” (Jude 21), and glory is given to God “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Jude 25). In Revelation he is “the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (1:5), “the First and the Last” (1:17), the Lamb who was slain (5:6), the rider called “Faithful and True” whose name is “The Word of God” (19:11, 13), and “the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star” (22:16). The book’s last promise is his: “Yes, I am coming soon” (22:20).
rel: The Lord Paul serves and the subject of the hymn

sub: Two men Paul says have shipwrecked their faith
bio: Paul says some have “rejected” a good conscience and “thereby shipwrecked their faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:19-20). The letter gives no further account of what they did. Names like these appear again in 2 Timothy: a Hymenaeus in 2:17 and an Alexander the coppersmith in 4:14, and the letters do not say whether they are the same men. In 2 Timothy Hymenaeus is named again, with Philetus (2:17-18), and Paul says, “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me” (4:14). The letters do not say whether the Alexanders are one man.
rel: Two named opponents at Ephesus

sub: The men Timothy is to instruct and correct
bio: Paul asks Timothy to “stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies” (1 Timothy 1:3-4). Some “want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying” (1:7). Later Paul says some “will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods” (4:3), and describes those who “regard godliness as a means of gain” (6:5). The letter does not name a school or a movement, and the readers disagree about who these men were. In 2 Timothy the same kind of teaching appears: Paul says to avoid “quarreling over words” (2:14) and warns that people “with itching ears” will “gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires” (4:3).
rel: Unnamed teachers inside the church

sub: The church as Paul describes it to Timothy
bio: Paul writes so “you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). The letter speaks to how it prays (2:1-8), who leads it (3:1-13), how it cares for widows (5:3-16) and how its members treat one another, including masters and slaves (6:1-2).
rel: The church at Ephesus

sub: Women the church was to honor and support
bio: Paul says, “Honor the widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy 5:3). A widow who is “truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God” (5:5). One “should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds” (5:9-10). Younger widows are not to be enrolled, and Paul advises them “to marry, have children, and manage their households” (5:11, 14). If “any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened” (5:16). What “enrolled” means, whether a list for support or an order of service, is debated.
rel: Women in need and women in service

sub: The relatives Paul says must care for their own
bio: Paul says that if a widow “has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents” (1 Timothy 5:4), and “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (5:8). The household was the first place of care, and the church was to help those who had no family (5:5, 16).
rel: The first circle of care

bio: Paul warns that “those who want to be rich” fall “into temptation” and that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:9-10). He tells Timothy to “instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God,” and to “be generous and ready to share” (6:17-18). The letter does not say they must give up what they have.
rel: Wealthy members of the church

sub: Those under the yoke and those they served
bio: Paul says that “all who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited,” and that those with “believing masters” are not to “show disrespect because they are brothers” (1 Timothy 6:1-2). The letter gives no instruction about freeing slaves. Many slaves were members of the early churches. Titus 2:9-10 asks slaves to submit, to be honest and well-pleasing, “so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.”
al: Those under the yoke of slavery
rel: Households divided by status but joined in the church

sub: The women Paul addresses in the instructions on prayer
bio: Paul says, “I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God” (1 Timothy 2:9-10). He then says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet” (2:12). Readers differ on what these verses meant in Ephesus and how they apply now, and on the meaning of “saved through childbearing” in 2:15. In 3:11 “the women” may be deacons’ wives or women deacons.
rel: Women in the church at Ephesus

bio: Paul writes of “your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well” (2 Timothy 1:5). They are named only here. Acts 16:1 says Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father was a Greek. Paul also says Timothy has known “the Holy Scriptures” “from infancy” (3:15), and the letter does not say who taught him, though the family is the likely answer. The letter does not say how the two women came to faith.
rel: Three generations of faith: Lois, Eunice, Timothy

sub: A friend who searched Rome for Paul
bio: Paul prays, “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me” (2 Timothy 1:16-17). He had also “ministered” to Paul “in Ephesus” (1:18). In 4:19 Paul greets “the household of Onesiphorus,” and Paul prays for the Lord to grant him mercy “on that day” (1:18), so some readers think he may have died, but the letter does not say. He is not named elsewhere in the New Testament.
rel: Ephesian friend who was not ashamed of the chains

sub: Two men from Asia who left Paul
bio: Paul says, “You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes” (2 Timothy 1:15). They are named only here, and the letter does not say what they did or why. Paul sets them beside Onesiphorus, who was “unashamed” of his chains (1:16).
rel: Men who left Paul at his time of need

sub: The next link in the chain of teaching
bio: Paul says, “the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The line has four links: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and “others.” The letter does not name the faithful men, and it does not say whether they were elders (compare 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9).
rel: Those who would teach after Timothy

sub: Two teachers whose talk spread “like gangrene”
bio: Paul says the talk of such men “will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some” (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Hymenaeus was named in 1 Timothy 1:20. Philetus appears only here. The letter does not explain what they meant by saying the resurrection had already occurred.
rel: Teachers at Ephesus who denied a future resurrection

sub: The kind of teacher Timothy is to be
bio: Paul says that “a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:24-25). The aim is that opponents “will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil” (2:26).
rel: Gentle in correcting, firm in the truth

bio: Paul says, “I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory” (2 Timothy 2:10). “The elect” means those whom God has chosen. The letter does not say who is meant in particular.
rel: The people God has chosen

sub: Men Paul says will be “lovers of themselves”
bio: Paul says, “In the last days terrible times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:1-2). They have “a form of godliness but denying its power,” and Timothy is to “turn away from such as these” (3:5). Later he writes that “evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived” (3:13).
rel: The false teachers and their followers

sub: Magicians who opposed Moses in Jewish tradition
bio: Paul says, “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth” (2 Timothy 3:8). The Old Testament does not name them, but Jewish tradition gave these names to the magicians of Pharaoh (Exodus 7:11). Paul adds that “their folly will be plain to everyone” (3:9).
rel: Pharaoh’s magicians in later tradition

sub: The man at Troas who kept Paul’s cloak
bio: Paul asks Timothy, “When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13). Carpus is named only here, and the letter says nothing more about him.
rel: Host or friend at Troas

sub: A co-worker who went to Galatia
bio: Paul says, “Crescens has gone to Galatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Some early manuscripts read “Gaul” instead. He is named only here.
rel: A worker sent or gone abroad

sub: A man who opposed Paul’s message
bio: Paul writes, “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message” (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Alexander was a common name. The letters do not say whether he is the Alexander of Acts 19:33 or of 1 Timothy 1:20.
rel: An opponent Timothy was to avoid

sub: An Ephesian companion left sick at Miletus
bio: Paul says, “Trophimus I left sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). Acts 20:4 names Trophimus among those from Asia who went with Paul, and Acts 21:29 calls him “the Ephesian.” The letter does not say what the illness was or when this happened.
rel: A friend from Ephesus

bio: Paul ends, “Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers” (2 Timothy 4:21). These four are named only here. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.3) names a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, but the letter does not say whether this is the same man.
rel: The church at Rome around Paul

sub: The region where Titus had gone
bio: Paul says, “Titus to Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Dalmatia was the Roman province on the east shore of the Adriatic, a part of the older Illyricum, which Paul names in Romans 15:19. The letter says nothing about why Titus went there.
rel: A province on the Adriatic

bio: Paul calls him “one of their own prophets” (Titus 1:12). Later writers name Epimenides as the poet behind the Cretan saying and describe him as a poet and seer from Crete, usually placed about 600 BC. The letter itself does not give his name.
rel: Cretan poet whose saying Paul quotes

sub: The people of the island and their reputation
bio: Paul quotes a saying about the people of the island: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (Titus 1:12). He says, “This testimony is true,” and tells Titus to “rebuke them sternly.” Cretans were among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and a ship carrying Paul put in at Fair Havens on Crete (Acts 27:7-12). Crete was a Roman province in Paul’s day. The letter tells Titus to appoint elders “in every town,” which suggests small groups of believers in several towns.
rel: People of Crete: a hard reputation and a mission field

bio: Paul says “many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision,” who “undermine entire households” for “dishonorable gain” (Titus 1:10-11). Their teaching included “Jewish myths” and “commands of men who have rejected the truth” (1:14). Titus is to silence them and rebuke them sternly. The letter does not say how many they were, or whether they were believers.
rel: Teachers of law and myth who divided churches

sub: Models for the rest of the church
bio: Paul tells Titus to teach “older men” to be “temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance” (Titus 2:2). “Older women” are to be “reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good” (2:3), and they can “train the young women” (2:4). Their teaching role grows out of their own conduct.
rel: Teaching by example in the household of God

sub: Taught by their elders and by Titus
bio: Younger women are trained “to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited” (Titus 2:4-5). Younger men are urged “to be self-controlled” (2:6). Paul’s stated aim is the reputation of the gospel among outsiders, and Titus himself is to be “an example by doing good works” (2:7).
rel: Younger believers taught to live the gospel

sub: One of the two men Paul might send
bio: Paul writes, “As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis” (Titus 3:12). Artemas is named only here. The letter does not say who he was, or whether he or Tychicus went to Crete.
rel: Possible replacement for Titus on Crete

sub: A traveler Titus is to equip
bio: Paul asks Titus, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need” (Titus 3:13). Zenas is named only here. In the New Testament “lawyer” usually means an expert in the law of Moses (Luke 7:30; 10:25), but the letter does not say what kind of lawyer he was.
rel: Law expert traveling with Apollos

sub: The person who is to be rejected after two warnings
bio: Paul writes, “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned” (Titus 3:10-11). He is not named, and the letter does not say what he taught beyond the “foolish controversies” and “quarrels about the law” of 3:9.
rel: Someone who causes factions in the church

sub: The slave owner Paul writes to
bio: Paul calls him “our beloved fellow worker” (Philemon 1) and thanks God for his “faith in the Lord Jesus” and “love for all the saints” (verse 5). The church met in his house (verse 2). He owned Onesimus, and Paul asks him to receive Onesimus back “as a beloved brother” (verse 16). Paul also says, “you owe me your very self” (verse 19), which suggests Paul had a part in Philemon’s own faith. The letter does not say where he lived. Colossians 4:9 and 4:17 point to Colossae. Church tradition, written down much later, makes him a bishop and a martyr, but the New Testament says nothing about the end of his life.
rel: Wealthy believer and slave owner at Colossae (probably)

bio: Paul greets “Apphia our sister” (Philemon 2). She is named only here. Many readers think she was Philemon’s wife, and the Greek word “sister” only means a fellow believer, so the letter does not say. She is greeted by name in the same verse as Archippus and the house church, so she was known to the church that met in the house.
rel: Believer greeted by name; perhaps Philemon’s wife

sub: The congregation the letter is read to
bio: Paul writes “to the church that meets at your house” (Philemon 2). Most of the letter says “you” in the singular to Philemon, but verses 3, 22 and 25 use the plural, so the whole church heard it read. Churches in homes are also found in Romans 16:5, 1 Corinthians 16:19 and Colossians 4:15. The letter does not say how large the group was.
rel: A congregation that met in a private home

sub: King of Salem and priest of God Most High
bio: Genesis 14:18-20 tells of him in three verses: he met Abraham after a battle, brought out bread and wine, and blessed him, and Abraham gave him a tenth. Psalm 110:4 says the Lord’s king is “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews 7 builds on these two passages. The writer reads his name as “king of righteousness” and “king of Salem” as “king of peace,” and notes that Genesis gives no father, mother or genealogy for him, so that he is “like the Son of God” and remains a priest for all time (7:1-3). Because Abraham gave him a tenth and was blessed by him, the writer argues that his priesthood is greater than the Levitical priesthood.
rel: Priest-king; a picture of the Son’s priesthood

sub: Moses’ brother, the first high priest
bio: Hebrews 5:4 says no one takes the honor of high priest on himself, but is called by God “just as Aaron was.” Aaron’s priesthood is the standard against which the writer sets Melchizedek (7:11), and Aaron’s budding rod is listed among the contents of the ark (9:4).
rel: First high priest of Israel

sub: Moses’ successor who led Israel into the land
bio: Hebrews 4:8 says that if Joshua had given Israel rest, God would not have spoken of another day. The writer takes this to mean that the entry under Joshua was not the final “rest,” which still lies ahead. Joshua is the Greek form Jesus, though the writer does not play on the two names here. The fall of Jericho under Joshua is named in 11:30.
rel: Led the people across the Jordan into the land

sub: The woman of Jericho who welcomed the spies
bio: Hebrews 11:31 says that Rahab the prostitute, “because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.” She is the only woman other than Sarah to be named in the list of the faithful in chapter 11, and James 2:25 also names her. Matthew 1:5 lists her in the genealogy of Jesus. James 2:25 asks whether even Rahab the prostitute was not justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route. She follows Abraham as a second example, a foreign woman beside the father of the nation.
rel: A foreigner who hid the spies and was spared

sub: The first three in the list of the faithful
bio: The list in chapter 11 begins with three men from Genesis. Abel offered “a better sacrifice than Cain” (11:4). Enoch “was taken up so that he did not see death” (11:5), and Noah, “in godly fear,” built an ark to save his family (11:7). The writer sets each beside the great pattern of faith: they acted on what God said before they saw it. 1 John 3:12 names Cain’s brother, whose deeds “were righteous,” though it does not give his name in the verse.
rel: Three men of Genesis who pleased God

sub: The faithful of chapter 11, seen as onlookers
bio: Hebrews 12:1 says “we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses.” The witnesses are the people just named in chapter 11, who testify by their lives to what faith is. The writer does not say that they can see the readers, only that their example surrounds them, and that the readers should look to Jesus, who “endured the cross, scorning its shame” (12:2).
rel: The faithful before Christ, as examples to the readers

n: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel
sub: Six names in the second half of the list of the faithful
bio: Hebrews 11:32 says there is not time to tell of “Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.” The four judges came first in Israel’s history, and the list is not in order of time. The writer then speaks in general of what faith achieved and what the faithful suffered (11:33-38). The list does not mention failures, though the stories in Judges and Samuel record them.
al: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel
rel: Judges, a king and a prophet named in a single sentence

n: The priests and the high priest
sub: The Levitical priests Hebrews compares with Christ
bio: Hebrews speaks of the priests who served under the law: the high priest taken from among men (5:1), the priests who went into the first room “continually” (9:6), and the great number of them, since death kept them from continuing (7:23). The writer says they served at a copy and shadow of heavenly things (8:4-5) and had to offer sacrifices again and again, and compares their service with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (10:11-12).
rel: Priests of the tribe of Levi under the law

sub: The community the letter is written to
bio: The letter does not say where its readers lived or who they were. It says they had been enlightened and had endured a hard struggle with sufferings, publicly exposed to abuse, and they had shared the lot of prisoners and accepted the loss of their possessions (10:32-34). They had shown love to the saints (6:10), but had grown “dull of hearing” (5:11), and some had stopped meeting together (10:25). The writer thinks better of them (6:9) and tells them to hold on. The title was added later, and most scholars take the readers to be Christians from a Jewish background, though some think the community included others.
rel: A tested community; place unknown, perhaps Rome

sub: Those who spoke the word of God to them and keep watch over them
bio: Hebrews 13:7 asks the readers to remember their leaders, who spoke the word of God to them, and to imitate their faith. Verse 17 asks them to obey and submit, since the leaders keep watch over their souls and will give an account. Verse 24 asks the readers to greet all of them. The letter does not name any of them.
rel: Church leaders at the readers’ end

sub: An unnamed teacher with a deep knowledge of Scripture
bio: The letter does not give its author’s name. The writer calls it “my word of exhortation” (13:22) and writes in some of the finest Greek in the New Testament, quoting the Greek Old Testament. He says Timothy has been released and sends greetings from “those from Italy.” He speaks of the message as “confirmed to us by those who heard Him” (2:3), so he was not one of the first hearers. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Priscilla and Luke have each been suggested; Origen, as Eusebius reports him, said only God knows.
rel: Unknown author; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others suggested

sub: Heavenly beings the Son is set above
bio: The first two chapters set the Son above the angels. They are “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (1:14), they were present when the law was given (2:2), and the Son was made for a little while lower than they (2:7). The writer also says that some have entertained angels without knowing it (13:2), and that at Mount Zion the readers have come to “myriads of angels” (12:22).
rel: Servants of God, below the Son

n: The twelve tribes of the Dispersion
sub: The scattered believers James writes to
bio: James is addressed “to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1). Dispersion (diaspora) was the word for Jews living outside the land, and the letter also says “your meeting” (2:2, a synagogue) and speaks of the Law and of Abraham, which fits readers from a Jewish background. Some take the phrase more widely, as a title for the whole church, like the “exiles of the Dispersion” in 1 Peter 1:1. The letter names no town. Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered after the death of Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and many readers think James has such people in mind.
rel: Jewish Christians, place unknown; Antioch in Syria is a common guess

bio: James 1:27 says that pure religion before God is to care for orphans and widows in their distress. They are the people the Law of Moses names again and again as needing protection, since they had no man of the household to speak for them or to provide (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21). The Greek verb translated “care for” is the word used for visiting the sick or the prisoner in Matthew 25.
rel: People with no one to provide for them

sub: Rich people in the assembly and outside it
bio: James speaks of the rich three times. The rich believer is told to take pride in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower (1:10-11). In the assembly the rich man in a gold ring is given the seat of honor, while the poor man is told to stand (2:2-3); James says it is the rich who drag the readers into court (2:6). At the end he calls on “you who are rich” to weep over the misery to come, since their wealth has rotted and the wages they held back are crying out (5:1-6). It is not clear whether the rich of chapter 5 are believers; the letter addresses them with the voice of a prophet and does not call them brothers.
rel: Warned in 1:10-11, 2:6 and 5:1-6

n: The poor and the lowly in James
bio: James says the brother “in humble circumstances” should be glad of his high position (1:9). The poor man in shabby clothes who is told to stand or to sit on the floor (2:2-3) is one of those God has chosen to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom (2:5), which echoes Jesus’ words “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20). James also says that to say “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed” to a person in need, without giving what the body needs, is worthless (2:15-16).
rel: The ones God has chosen to be rich in faith

sub: Those who teach in the assembly
bio: James begins chapter 3 by saying that not many should become teachers, since “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (3:1). He includes himself with “we,” so the writer is a teacher. A teacher had a place of honor among the early believers, and the tongue was his tool, which is why the rest of the chapter is about its power.
rel: Judged more strictly

bio: James asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you?” and answers that such a person shows it by good conduct and by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom (3:13). He says that jealousy and selfish ambition are not wisdom, and that the wisdom from above is pure, peace-loving, gentle, full of mercy and good fruit (3:14-17).
rel: Wisdom shown by good conduct

sub: Those God opposes and those he lifts up
bio: Quoting Proverbs 3:34, James says “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (4:6). He asks the double-minded to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts, to grieve and mourn, and to humble themselves before the Lord, who “will exalt you” (4:8-10). Jesus says nearly the same thing in Matthew 23:12.
rel: Opposed by God, or given grace

sub: Traders who plan a year ahead
bio: James addresses those who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit” (4:13). He does not condemn trade but the boast that leaves God out. Life is “a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (4:14), and they ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that” (4:15).
rel: Traders who forget that life is a mist

bio: James tells his readers to be patient “until the Lord’s coming,” and “See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains” (5:7). The farmer sows after the early rain of autumn and waits for the late rain of spring before the harvest, and cannot hurry either.
rel: Waits for the early and late rains

sub: The sufferer of the book of Job
bio: James 5:11 says, “You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.” Job is named only here in the New Testament. In the Old Testament Job also complains and questions God, but James picks out what he endured and the way the story ends. A Jewish writing called the Testament of Job, from about the same period, also makes Job a model of endurance.
rel: Held up for his endurance

n: The believers of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia
bio: The letter is addressed “to the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1). These were five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, today most of Turkey. Peter calls them “foreigners and exiles” (2:11), a “chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (2:9), and “God’s flock” (5:2). They were being slandered as evildoers (2:12) and were put to shame for no longer joining in the life of their neighbors (4:4). Whether they were mostly Jewish or mostly Gentile in background is debated; the letter reminds them of their “empty way of life” (1:18) and of “the same desires as the Gentiles” (4:3), which points to Gentile converts. The second letter is addressed “to those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours” (2 Peter 1:1), and calls itself “my second letter to you” (3:1). Many take the readers to be the same churches as in 1 Peter; the letter does not name them.
rel: Scattered believers, called a chosen people

n: The prophets of the old covenant
sub: Those who searched for the salvation Peter proclaims
bio: Peter says the prophets “searched and investigated carefully” about this salvation, “trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (1:10-11). They were “not serving themselves, but you” (1:12). The letter quotes Isaiah, Psalms, Proverbs, Hosea, Leviticus and Exodus, and the picture of the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 shapes chapter 2. 2 Peter 1:19-21 says “the word of the prophets” is “a lamp shining in a dark place,” and that “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” 3:2 speaks of what was foretold “by the holy prophets.”
rel: Searched for the time and the setting

bio: Peter tells “servants” (the Greek oiketai, household slaves) to “submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable” (2:18). He says the pain of unjust suffering is “to be commended” when borne by one who is conscious of God (2:19), and points them to Christ, who suffered and left an example. Slaves were a large part of any Roman city. Peter does not tell them to seek freedom, and he does not argue about slavery as an institution; he speaks as well of the dignity of the believing slave, who is a “servant of God” (2:16).
rel: Told to follow Christ’s example in unjust suffering

sub: The non-Christian neighbors who watched and spoke against the readers
bio: Peter tells his readers to “conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us” (2:12). The same neighbors “consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you” (4:4). They are not named, and the letter does not describe any trial before a court; the pressure is social, with ridicule, exclusion and insult.
rel: Slander now; perhaps glory to God later

sub: The old companions who now heap abuse
bio: In chapter 4 Peter says that the readers “have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry” (4:3). Their old friends are surprised that they no longer join in and “heap abuse on you” (4:4). The letter says they “will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” (4:5).
rel: Surprised, and abusive

bio: Peter writes to wives first, “so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives” (3:1), and says that their beauty should come not from “braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes” but “from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit” (3:3-4). He holds up the holy women of the past who “put their hope in God” (3:5), among them Sarah. To husbands he says, “treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered” (3:7).
rel: Called to honor and to purity of life

bio: Peter recalls “the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water” (3:20). He pairs the flood with baptism: “this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also” (3:21). Peter does not name the mountains where the ark came to rest. Genesis 8:4 puts it on the mountains of Ararat. 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah a preacher of righteousness. 2 Peter 2:5 calls him “a preacher of righteousness” and says God “preserved” him “among the eight” when He brought the flood on the ungodly world, and 3:5-6 recalls that the world “perished in the flood.”
rel: Eight souls saved through water

sub: The God Peter tells the readers to trust
bio: Peter ends chapter 4 by saying that “those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good” (4:19). Elsewhere in the letter God is the Father who foreknew (1:2), who raised Christ from the dead (1:3, 1:21), who “judges each one’s work impartially” (1:17), who “opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (5:5) and who is “the God of all grace” (5:10).
rel: Faithful, and the God of all grace

sub: The two who share the closing greeting
bio: Peter writes “through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother” (5:12) and sends greetings from the church in Babylon and from “my son Mark” (5:13). Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion, named with Timothy in the greetings of 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Mark is almost certainly John Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, who first went with Paul and then with Barnabas, and who was later with Paul in Rome (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). Early writers said that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, and that his Gospel keeps Peter’s preaching.
rel: Silvanus carried or wrote the letter; Mark is “my son”

bio: Peter tells his readers to “submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right” (2:13-14). He ends with “Fear God, honor the king” (2:17). The king meant the Roman emperor, who in the early 60s was Nero. The governors were the officials he sent to the provinces. Peter does not name either.
rel: Honored, but not feared

sub: The people the elders are to shepherd
bio: Peter tells the elders to “be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you” (5:2). They are not to be “lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (5:3). The picture is that of Ezekiel 34 and of John 21:15-17, where the risen Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep. The “Chief Shepherd” is Christ, who is also “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25).
rel: The sheep of the Chief Shepherd

bio: The letter says “there will be false teachers among you,” who “will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them” (2:1). It says they are driven by greed and exploit the readers “with deceptive words” (2:3), that they “despise authority” and “slander glorious beings” (2:10), that they carouse and are “reveling in their deception as they feast with you” (2:13), and that they “promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity” (2:19). The letter does not name them or their teaching. Much of the chapter follows the letter of Jude, which speaks of ungodly people who have slipped in. Scholars have suggested early forms of Gnostic or libertine teaching, or teachers who denied the coming judgment, and the scoffers of 3:3-4 may be the same people. Jude calls such people “certain men” who “have crept in among you unnoticed” (Jude 4).
rel: Warned against; compared with Balaam

sub: Those who ask where the promise is
bio: Peter says that “in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires” (3:3). They ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” and say, “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation” (3:4). The letter answers that they “deliberately overlook” creation and the flood (3:5-6), and that the delay is God’s patience (3:9). Jude 18 uses the same word for mockers. The letter does not say who they were or whether they were inside or outside the church. Jude 18 gives the apostles’ warning in nearly the same words: “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.”
rel: Mock the promise of Christ’s coming

sub: Those who heard the voice on the holy mountain
bio: The writer says “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” and “we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (1:16-18). The Gospels name Peter, James and John as the three disciples Jesus took up the mountain (Matthew 17:1; Mark 9:2; Luke 9:28). The letter does not name the mountain.
