rel: Peter, James and John

sub: The seer who loved the wages of wickedness
bio: A seer from Pethor on the Euphrates whom the king of Moab hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24). His donkey saw the angel of the LORD and spoke, and instead of cursing he blessed Israel. Numbers 31:16 says his advice led Israel into sin at Peor, and Revelation 2:14 speaks of the teaching of Balaam. Peter says the false teachers “have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness” (2:15-16). Jude 11 also mentions Balaam’s error. A wall inscription from Deir ‘Alla, about 800 BC, names a seer called Balaam son of Beor. Jude’s words are, “they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam” (Jude 11). Revelation 2:14 speaks of “the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the Israelites so they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality.”
rel: Rebuked by a donkey

bio: Abraham’s nephew, who chose the plain of the Jordan and settled near Sodom, and who was led out of the city before it was destroyed (Genesis 13; 19). Genesis does not call him righteous, but 2 Peter does: God “rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)” (2:7-8). The letter uses him to show that “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials” (2:9). Jesus joined the days of Noah and the days of Lot (Luke 17:26-30).
rel: Nephew of Abraham

bio: The letter says “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2:4). It does not say what they did. Most readers link the verse to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Jewish Book of Enoch, where rebel angels are bound until the judgment; Jude 6 says almost the same. Some take it to mean the fall of Satan and his angels. The Greek verb is from Tartarus, the prison of the underworld in Greek writing. Jude 6 reads, “the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.”
rel: Held for judgment

bio: The letter does not give a name. It speaks in the first person plural of what “we have heard, … seen with our own eyes, … gazed upon and touched with our own hands” (1:1), and in the singular as “I am writing” (2:1). From the second century, church writers such as Irenaeus say that it came from John the apostle, who lived at Ephesus. The Second and Third Letters are written by “the elder,” and Papias mentions a John the Elder, so some scholars think that was the writer; others hold that the apostle is meant. The letter also leaves out any greeting and any closing.
al: John, the writer of the letters
rel: Called John by early tradition

sub: Those who heard, saw and touched
bio: The letter opens with “we”: “which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life” (1:1). They “testified to it” and “proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father” (1:2). Most readers take this to be the apostles, or the apostolic circle, who knew Jesus in his earthly life. In 4:14 the same voice says “we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.”
al: The eyewitnesses of the Word of life
rel: Apostolic witnesses

bio: The letter does not name a church or a city. It speaks to its readers as “my little children” (2:1), “beloved” (2:7; 3:2; 4:1), and “brothers” (3:13), and says it writes “to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). Since the second century, readers have placed them in the churches around Ephesus in the province of Asia. They have been shaken by teachers who left their fellowship.
rel: Addressed as children and beloved

bio: In a pair of three-line verses the writer says: “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one” (2:12-13). He repeats them with “I have written” in 2:14. Some take the three words to mean ages of life; others take them to mean three stages of Christian growth, or the whole church under three names.
al: Little children, fathers and young men
rel: Addressed in 2:12-14

n: Those who went out from us
sub: The teachers who left the fellowship
bio: The letter says “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us” (2:19). It calls them liars who deny “that Jesus is the Christ” (2:22) and “those who are trying to deceive you” (2:26), and says they do not confess “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2). It does not give their names or spell out their teaching. Some scholars think of Cerinthus, others of an early form of docetism, which held that Christ only seemed to have a body; the evidence is debated. 2 John 7 speaks of “many deceivers” who “have gone out into the world,” which many readers link with the group that “went out from us” in 1 John 2:19.
al: Those who went out from us
rel: Left the community; denied the Son

n: The antichrist and the many antichrists
bio: The word “antichrist” appears in the New Testament only in 1 John (2:18, 22; 4:3) and 2 John 7. The letter says, “just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared” (2:18), and defines the antichrist as the one “who denies the Father and the Son” (2:22). In 4:3 “the spirit of the antichrist” is “already in the world at this time.” The writer sees the mark of the antichrist in a present denial, not in a single figure in the future. 2 John 7 repeats the word: “Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.”
rel: Deny that Jesus is the Christ

n: The false prophets and the spirits
bio: The letter tells its readers, “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world” (4:1). The test is whether the spirit “confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2). The writer adds, “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception” (4:6).
rel: Tested by their confession

bio: The first son of Adam and Eve, who brought an offering from the ground, was angry when God looked with favor on his brother Abel’s offering, and killed him in the field (Genesis 4:1-16). God marked him and sent him to wander. In the New Testament he is named in Hebrews 11:4, Jude 11 and 1 John 3:12, which says he “belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous.” Jude says of the intruders, “They have traveled the path of Cain” (Jude 11).
rel: Murdered his brother Abel

n: The children of God and the children of the devil
sub: Two families, told apart by what they do
bio: The letter says, “By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother” (3:10). It opens the chapter with “we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!” (3:1), and in 3:8 says “The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start.”
rel: Known by righteousness and love

bio: The letter says, “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One” (2:1). The Greek word is paraklētos, the word the Gospel of John uses of the Holy Spirit as “Helper” (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7); it occurs five times in the New Testament, four in the Gospel and here. The next verse calls Him “the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (2:2).
rel: Pleads for those who sin

sub: The writer, who gives no name
bio: The letter opens “The elder” (1:1) and gives no other name, and the Third Letter opens the same way. Church writers from the second century on, Irenaeus among them, quote 2 John as the work of John, the Lord’s disciple. Papias, a bishop at Hierapolis, spoke of an elder named John besides the apostle, and some scholars think this elder wrote the Second and Third Letters; others hold that the apostle called himself “the elder” as an older man with standing in the churches. He loves the readers “in the truth” (1:1), is “overjoyed” to find their children “walking in the truth” (1:4), and hopes “to come and speak with you face to face” (1:12). 3 John opens the same way, “The elder, To the beloved Gaius” (3 John 1). There he speaks of “my children,” says he has “written to the church,” plans a visit, and expects to deal with Diotrephes when he comes (3 John 4, 9-10, 14). Whether this elder also wrote Revelation is an old question. The writer of Revelation calls himself John and never “the elder.”
al: The elder of 2 John and 3 John
rel: Writes as “the elder”; called John by early tradition

n: The chosen lady and her children
bio: The letter is addressed to “the chosen lady and her children” (1:1). Most readers take the lady to be a local church and her children its members, because verse 13 sends greetings from “the children of your elect sister,” and because the letter turns to a plural “you” in verses 6, 8, 10 and 12. Others think a real woman who led a church in her home is meant, and a few take Kyria or Electa as her name. The letter does not say where she lived. The writer loves her “in the truth,” urges her to love one another (1:5), and tells her not to “receive him into your home” if he does not bring the teaching of Christ (1:10).
al: The elect lady and her children
rel: Addressed in 1:1 and 1:5

n: The children of the chosen sister
bio: The letter ends, “The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (1:13). The sister is usually read as the church where the writer is, and her children as its members. The letter does not say where it is. The word for “elect” (eklektē) is the same one used for the lady in verse 1.
al: The children of your elect sister
rel: Send greetings in 1:13

sub: Those who refuse to confess Jesus Christ in the flesh
bio: The letter says, “many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist” (1:7). It also describes people who run ahead “without remaining in the teaching of Christ” (1:9) and who bring a different teaching to a house (1:10). The writer does not name them or describe what they taught beyond this. Many readers link them with the teachers who “went out from us” in 1 John 2:19, and early writers such as Irenaeus and Ignatius point to those who said Christ only seemed to have a body, or who separated the man Jesus from the Christ.
rel: Deny the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh

sub: The guests who needed a home
bio: Early Christian teachers, prophets and workers moved from church to church and depended on Christian households for food and a bed. The Third Letter praises those who welcomed such brothers, and the Didache gives rules for receiving them. 2 John uses this setting: a visitor who “does not bring this teaching” is not to be received “into your home or even greet him” (1:10). The letter does not tell the readers to refuse everyone who disagrees with them; its test is what a visitor teaches about Christ. 3 John shows the custom from the other side. Gaius is praised for what he does “for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (3 John 5), and the elder says, “we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8).
rel: Visitors who may or may not bring the teaching

n: Gaius, the friend the elder writes to
bio: The letter is addressed “To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” (1:1), and it calls him “Beloved” three more times. Brothers who visited him “testified about your devotion to the truth” (1:3), and he is “faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (1:5). The elder may count him among “my children” (1:4). He belongs to a church in which Diotrephes has refused the brothers, and the elder asks him to keep on receiving them and to “send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (1:6). Gaius was a very common Roman name. The New Testament has a Gaius of Macedonia, a Gaius of Derbe and a Gaius of Corinth, and nothing shows that this is any of them. A church manual of about AD 380 calls a Gaius the bishop of Pergamum, a late tradition that cannot be checked.
rel: Friend, and perhaps convert, of the elder

sub: The man who loves to be first
bio: A leading man in the church the elder wrote to. The letter says, “Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction” (1:9). The elder charges him with “malicious slander against us,” and says that “he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church” (1:10). The letter does not accuse him of false teaching; the complaint is about ambition and the way he treats others. Readers differ over what he was: the host of a house church, a leader who had taken sole control, or a man who distrusted outsiders. His name means nourished by Zeus and is rare. He is known only from these two verses.
al: Diotrephes, who loves to be first
rel: Opposes the elder; refuses the traveling brothers

sub: The man with a good testimony
bio: The elder writes, “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true” (1:12). He is probably the man who carried the letter to Gaius, and perhaps one of the traveling brothers, so that the verse works as a letter of recommendation. Nothing links him with the silversmith Demetrius of Acts 19, and the name was common. A church manual of about AD 380 makes a Demetrius the bishop of Philadelphia, a late tradition that cannot be checked.
rel: Commended by the elder to Gaius

sub: Workers who went out for the Name
bio: Christian workers who traveled from church to church. They were “strangers” to Gaius when he took them in (1:5), and afterward “They have testified to the church about your love” (1:6). The elder says, “they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (1:7-8). Diotrephes “refuses to welcome the brothers” (1:10). They are not named, unless Demetrius is one of them, and the letter does not say where they were going.
rel: Sent from the elder’s church; received by Gaius, refused by Diotrephes

sub: Believers with the elder and with Gaius
bio: The letter ends, “The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name” (1:14). “The friends” are the believers around the elder and those around Gaius. It is a rare name for Christians in the New Testament; in the Gospel of John Jesus tells his disciples that he calls them friends. Greeting each one by name fits a small circle in which everyone was known.
rel: Send and receive greetings in 1:14

sub: Writer of the letter of Jude
bio: The letter opens, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (1:1). Jude is the same name as Judas and Judah. Most readers take him to be the Judas whom the Gospels list among the brothers of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55), and the James he names to be the leader of the church in Jerusalem. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and does not mention the family tie. He does not claim to be an apostle and speaks of “the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ” as others (1:17). He had meant to write “about the salvation we share,” but “felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith” (1:3). He knows the Old Testament well and also uses two Jewish books outside it. The brothers of Jesus did not believe in him during his ministry, were among the believers after the resurrection, and later traveled as missionaries. Hegesippus, in the 2nd century, tells of two grandsons of Jude who farmed in the land of Israel and were questioned under Domitian. Some scholars think the letter was written later in his name.
al: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ
rel: Brother of James, and by the usual reading a brother of Jesus

bio: The letter is written “To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ” (1:1). No town or region is named. They are “Beloved” three times (1:3, 17, 20), they share a common salvation with Jude, they hold love feasts (1:12), and apostles had taught them (1:17-18). They know the stories of the Old Testament well enough to need only a reminder (1:5), which points to a church with deep Jewish roots. Jude tells them to keep themselves “in the love of God” (1:21) and to “have mercy on those who doubt” (1:22), and he ends with praise to the God “who is able to keep you from stumbling” (1:24).
al: Those who are called, loved and kept
rel: Taught by apostles; troubled by intruders

n: The ungodly men who crept in
bio: Jude writes, “certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (1:4). He calls them “these dreamers” who “defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings” (1:8). They are “hidden reefs in your love feasts” (1:12), “discontented grumblers” who “flatter others for their own advantage” (1:16), and people “who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit” (1:19). Jude never names them or sets out their teaching. They seem to have been traveling teachers who claimed visions and taught that grace set believers free from moral rules. Later writers linked them with Gnostic groups, but the letter itself shows only their way of life. 2 Peter 2 describes its false teachers in much the same words.
rel: Slipped in among the readers of Jude

bio: Jude writes, “even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’” (1:9). The name means “Who is like God?” In the book of Daniel he is the great prince who stands guard over Israel (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1), and in Revelation 12:7 he and his angels fight the dragon. Jewish writings of the time count him among the chief angels. The story of the body of Moses is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers say Jude took it from a Jewish book called the Assumption of Moses. Only here in the Bible is Michael called “the archangel,” and the only other use of that word is 1 Thessalonians 4:16. In Revelation 12:7 “Michael and his angels fought against the dragon,” and the dragon was thrown down to the earth.
rel: Disputes with the devil over the body of Moses

bio: A Levite of the family of Kohath who, with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders, rose against Moses and Aaron and claimed that the whole community was holy and needed no such leaders (Numbers 16:1-3). The ground opened and swallowed the rebels, and fire consumed the 250 who offered incense (Numbers 16:31-35). His sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), and several psalms carry the name of the sons of Korah. Jude says of the intruders, “they have perished in Korah’s rebellion” (1:11): they reject authority in the church as he did, and Jude speaks of their end as certain.
rel: Rebelled against Moses and Aaron

sub: The man who walked with God
bio: Enoch is the seventh name in the family line from Adam through Seth (Genesis 5:3-18). Genesis says that he walked with God and that God took him (Genesis 5:24), and Hebrews 11:5 says he was taken up so that he did not see death. In the centuries before Jesus a large body of Jewish writing grew up under his name, telling of his journeys through heaven and his warnings of judgment. Jude quotes from it: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: ‘Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone’” (1:14-15). The words are from 1 Enoch 1:9. Jude is the only New Testament writer to quote the book by name.
rel: Son of Jared, father of Methuselah

n: Those who doubt and those in the fire
bio: Near its end the letter turns to members of the church who have been unsettled: “have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh” (1:22-23). The first group wavers, the second has gone further and needs quick rescue, and the third is to be helped with care so that the helper is not drawn in. The Greek copies differ in these verses, and some have only two groups. The pictures of fire and stained clothing come from Zechariah 3:2-4. Jude is hard on the intruders and gentle with those they have misled.
rel: Members of the church to be shown mercy

bio: The writer names himself four times as John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8) and gives himself no title but servant, brother and prophet: “I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9). He knows the seven churches of Asia closely and expects them to accept his authority. His mind is soaked in the Old Testament; he never quotes it formally, yet most verses echo it. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, in the 2nd century, say he was John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, and that is the main tradition of the church. Dionysius of Alexandria, in the 3rd century, pointed to the differences in Greek style between Revelation and the Gospel of John and concluded that another John wrote it; many modern scholars agree, and some speak of a prophet John otherwise unknown. Early writers say he was banished to Patmos under Domitian and later returned to Ephesus.
rel: Brother and fellow servant of the seven churches; by tradition the apostle John

bio: John is told, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea” (1:11). The seven cities lay on a loop of road in the Roman province of Asia, in the order a messenger from Patmos would reach them. There were other churches in the province, such as Colossae and Troas, so the seven stand for the whole church; seven is the number of completeness in this book. Each is pictured as a golden lampstand with Christ walking among them (1:20; 2:1). Their conditions differ. Smyrna and Philadelphia are poor, pressed and praised. Ephesus is sound and loveless. Pergamum and Thyatira are faithful but put up with false teaching. Sardis is nearly dead, and Laodicea is rich and self-satisfied. Every letter ends, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”
rel: Addressed by Christ through John

n: The angels of the seven churches
sub: The seven stars in Christ’s hand
bio: Each of the seven letters is addressed “To the angel of the church” in a city, and Christ explains that “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches” (1:20). Who they are is debated. They may be heavenly angels who represent or guard each church, as nations have angels in Daniel 10. They may be human messengers or leaders, since the Greek word also means messenger. Or the angel may be a way of speaking of the church itself, its spirit or character, which would explain why the angel is praised and blamed for what the church does. Everywhere else in Revelation the word means a heavenly being.
rel: Held in the right hand of Christ

sub: A group in the churches of Asia
bio: The church at Ephesus is praised: “You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (2:6). At Pergamum some hold their teaching, which is set beside “the teaching of Balaam,” who led Israel to “eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality” (2:14-15). The prophetess at Thyatira taught the same (2:20). They seem to have been Christians who argued that believers could take part in the feasts of the trade guilds and the city, where the meat came from the temples and the emperor and the gods were honored. Paul dealt with a similar question at Corinth (1 Corinthians 8-10). Irenaeus and later writers traced the group to Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but they may only have been guessing from the name.
al: Those who hold the teaching of Balaam
rel: Opposed at Ephesus; tolerated at Pergamum

bio: Christ says to the church at Pergamum, “you have held fast to My name and have not denied your faith in Me, even in the day when My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you, where Satan dwells” (2:13). Nothing else is known of him. He is the only person in the seven churches named as having died for the faith, and he is given the title that 1:5 gives to Jesus, “the faithful witness.” The Greek word for witness is martys, and from deaths like his it came to mean martyr. A later legend says he was bishop of Pergamum and was burned inside a bronze bull.
rel: A member of the church at Pergamum

sub: A teacher in the church at Thyatira
bio: Christ says to Thyatira, “You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols” (2:20). Jezebel is almost certainly not her real name. It is the name of the queen of Israel who promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted the prophets (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 21:25). The woman at Thyatira was a Christian with a following in the church who claimed to speak for God, and she taught that believers could join in the meals of the guilds and their gods. Women did prophesy in the early churches (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5); the fault found here is what she taught. She had been given time to repent and refused.
rel: Tolerated by the church at Thyatira

sub: Those who stay faithful to the end
bio: Each of the seven letters ends with a promise “To the one who overcomes.” The Greek verb is nikaō, to conquer or win, from the word for victory. The promises are the tree of life, safety from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star, white clothing and a name kept in the Book of Life, a place as a pillar in God’s temple, and a seat on Christ’s throne: “just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne” (3:21). All of them return in chapters 20-22. The book shows how the victory is won. The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5-6), and his people conquer the dragon “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11). In Revelation to overcome is to stay faithful, if need be to death.
rel: Believers in the seven churches and in every place

sub: Enthroned around the throne of God
bio: John sees that “Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads” (4:4). They fall down before God, lay their crowns before the throne, hold harps and bowls of incense, sing the new song to the Lamb, and one of them twice explains to John what he sees (5:5; 7:13-14). Their number has been explained as twelve tribes and twelve apostles, the whole people of God in both covenants, whose names are on the gates and foundations of the new Jerusalem (21:12-14). Others see the twenty-four orders of priests and singers in 1 Chronicles 24-25, and others an order of angels, a heavenly council like that of Isaiah 24:23.
rel: Worship God and the Lamb

sub: Around the throne, never ceasing to praise
bio: Around the throne are four living creatures, covered with eyes, the first like a lion, the second like an ox, the third with a face like a man, the fourth like a flying eagle. “Day and night they never stop saying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’” (4:8). They combine the four-faced cherubim of Ezekiel 1 and 10 with the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6. They lead the worship of heaven, call out the four horsemen (6:1-7), and hand the seven bowls to the angels (15:7). They are usually taken to stand for the whole living creation praising its Maker. From the 2nd century Christians also used them as signs of the four Gospels: in the best-known scheme the man is Matthew, the lion Mark, the ox Luke and the eagle John.
rel: Nearest the throne of God

sub: Jesus Christ as John sees him
bio: John hears of a Lion and turns to see a Lamb: “Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne” (5:6). From then on “the Lamb” is the book’s chief name for Jesus, used 28 times. The picture joins the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) and John the Baptist’s “Lamb of God.” The Lamb has been killed and stands alive. He alone can open the scroll of God’s purposes, he is worshiped with God (5:13), he shepherds his people (7:17), the kings make war on him and he defeats them, he has a bride, and with God he is the temple and the lamp of the new Jerusalem (21:22-23). Heaven sings, “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” (5:12).
al: The Lion of the tribe of Judah
rel: Jesus Christ, shown as the slain and living Lamb

sub: Riders of the first four seals
bio: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders are called out. The first rides a white horse, holds a bow and is given a crown, “and he rode out to overcome and conquer” (6:2). The second, on a red horse, takes peace from the earth. The third, on a black horse, holds scales, and a voice names famine prices for wheat and barley. The fourth is on a pale green horse: “Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind” (6:8). They are given authority over a quarter of the earth. The horses come from Zechariah 1 and 6. The riders are conquest, war, famine and death, the troubles Jesus called “the beginning of birth pains.” Some readers take the first rider as Christ or the gospel going out, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11; most take him as conquest, like the other three.
al: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse
rel: Sent out when the Lamb opens the seals

sub: Those slain for the word of God
bio: At the fifth seal John sees “under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld. And they cried out in a loud voice, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?’” (6:9-10). Each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer. They appear again as those who conquered the beast (15:2), as the blood found in Babylon (17:6; 18:24), and as the souls who come to life and reign with Christ (20:4). Revelation treats their deaths as victories and their prayer for justice as one God will answer.
rel: Killed for their testimony to Jesus

bio: John hears “the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel” (7:4), twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. They are marked on the forehead as God’s own before the judgments fall. They appear again on Mount Zion with the Lamb, with his name and his Father’s name on their foreheads: “They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb” (14:4). Some readers take them as Jewish believers. Others take the number as a picture of the whole church as God’s army, counted like the tribes in the book of Numbers, and identify them with the countless multitude that John sees straight afterward. The group known as Jehovah’s Witnesses takes the number literally, as those who will reign in heaven.
al: The servants of God sealed on their foreheads
rel: Sealed by God; companions of the Lamb

sub: From every nation, before the throne
bio: After the 144,000 are numbered, John sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands” (7:9). An elder explains: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). They serve God day and night, and the Lamb is their shepherd. A great multitude is heard again in 19:1-6, shouting “Hallelujah!” at the fall of Babylon and the wedding of the Lamb.
al: The multitude no one could count
Those who come out of the great tribulation
rel: The redeemed of all nations

bio: A voice says, “I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth” (11:3). “These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth” (11:4), a picture from Zechariah 4. Fire comes from their mouths, they can shut the sky and turn water to blood, as Elijah and Moses did. When they finish, the beast from the Abyss kills them; their bodies lie in the street of the great city for three and a half days while the world celebrates; then God raises them and calls them up to heaven. Readers have taken them as Moses and Elijah, as Enoch and Elijah (who did not die), as two prophets of the last days, as the Law and the Prophets, or as the church bearing witness, since two is the number of witnesses the law requires (Deuteronomy 19:15).
rel: Killed by the beast and raised by God

n: The woman clothed with the sun
sub: Mother of the child the dragon hunts
bio: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (12:1). She is in labor, and a dragon waits to devour her child, who is “a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter” (12:5), the Messiah. The child is caught up to God, and she flees to the wilderness, where God feeds her. The dragon then makes war on “the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus” (12:17). The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream about the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9). Most readers take her as the people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah came, and the church, his persecuted family. In Catholic and Orthodox tradition she is also Mary, the mother of Jesus.
al: A woman clothed in the sun
rel: Mother of the male child; pursued by the dragon

sub: The devil, as Revelation pictures him
bio: John sees an enormous red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven crowns, whose tail sweeps a third of the stars from the sky. He is named plainly: “the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9). He tries to devour the Messiah at his birth, loses a war in heaven to Michael, and is thrown down to earth, where he pursues the woman and her children. He gives his power and throne to the beast from the sea (13:2), and with the beast and the false prophet he forms a counterfeit of God, the Lamb and the Spirit. He is bound for a thousand years, released, and at last thrown into the lake of fire (20:10). In the Old Testament the sea monster Leviathan or Rahab stands for the powers of chaos that God defeats (Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:13-14).
al: The deceiver of the whole world
rel: Satan; the power behind the two beasts

bio: “Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads” (13:1). It looks like a leopard with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth, the four beasts of Daniel 7 in one. The dragon gives it his power; one of its heads has a mortal wound that has healed; the whole earth worships it; it makes war on the saints for 42 months. Its number is 666 (13:18). It carries the prostitute Babylon and later destroys her (17:3, 16), and it is captured by the rider on the white horse and thrown into the lake of fire (19:20). John’s first readers would have seen in it the Roman Empire and its emperors, who were given divine titles. Many readers also, or instead, see a final ruler at the end of the age, the Antichrist, a name Revelation itself does not use.
rel: Empowered by the dragon; worshiped by the earth

n: The beast from the earth, the false prophet
sub: Makes the world worship the first beast
bio: “Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon” (13:11). It acts for the first beast, works signs, has an image of the beast made, and sees to it that no one can buy or sell without the beast’s mark. Later it is called “the false prophet” (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), and it shares the first beast’s end. Where the first beast is power, the second is persuasion: religion and propaganda in the service of the state. For the churches of Asia this was the network of priests and officials who ran the worship of the emperor. Jesus warned of false prophets who would work great signs (Matthew 24:24).
rel: Servant of the first beast

sub: The great city, pictured as a prostitute
bio: John sees a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, seated on a scarlet beast, drunk with the blood of the saints. “And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH” (17:5). An angel explains that she sits on seven mountains and that she “is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth” (17:18). Chapter 18 is a funeral song over her: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (18:2). Kings, merchants and sailors mourn the loss of her trade, and God’s people are told to come out of her. Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. For John’s first readers the name pointed to Rome, the city on seven hills, which destroyed Jerusalem again in AD 70. Other readings take her as unfaithful Jerusalem, as a world power still to come, or as human society organized without God in any age. She is the opposite of the bride, the new Jerusalem.
al: The woman on the scarlet beast
rel: Carried by the beast; destroyed by it

sub: Those who grew rich from Babylon
bio: Three groups stand at a distance and lament the burning of Babylon. The kings of the earth, who shared her luxury, weep first. Then “the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo” (18:11), and John lists the cargo, from gold to slaves. Last come the shipmasters and sailors, throwing dust on their heads. Each group cries “Woe, woe” and marvels that she fell in a single hour. None of them mourns for her people; they mourn their own losses. The passage follows Ezekiel 26-27, the lament for the trading city of Tyre.
al: Those who make their living from the sea
rel: Partners in Babylon’s trade

n: The bride, the wife of the Lamb
sub: The people of God as a city
bio: Heaven announces, “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready” (19:7). Her fine linen “is the righteous acts of the saints” (19:8). When an angel says, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb” (21:9), John is shown a city: “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (21:2). The bride is the whole people of God, joined to Christ forever, and the city is where God lives with them. The picture comes from the prophets, who call God the husband of Israel (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19), and from Paul (Ephesians 5:25-32). At the end “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (22:17).
rel: Joined to the Lamb

sub: The nations gathered for the last battle
bio: After the thousand years Satan goes out “to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore” (20:8). They surround the camp of the saints, and fire from heaven consumes them. In Ezekiel 38-39 Gog is a prince of the land of Magog who leads a great army from the far north against Israel and is destroyed by God. Magog is a grandson of Noah in Genesis 10:2. In Revelation the two names together stand for all the hostile nations of the world. Attempts to identify them with particular modern countries have changed with every generation and have no basis in the text.
rel: Deceived and gathered by Satan

n: Abaddon, the angel of the Abyss
sub: King of the locusts of the fifth trumpet
bio: The locusts that rise from the Abyss at the fifth trumpet “were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon” (9:11). Abaddon means destruction, and in the Old Testament it is a name for the realm of the dead (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11). Apollyon means destroyer. Some think John chose the Greek name to recall Apollo, the god the emperor Domitian favored, one of whose signs was the locust. He may be the same as Satan or one of Satan’s angels; the text does not say. John Bunyan made Apollyon the fiend whom Christian fights in The Pilgrim’s Progress.
rel: King over the locusts from the Abyss

n: Those who dwell on the earth
sub: Revelation’s name for a world against God
bio: The phrase “those who dwell on the earth” comes about ten times in Revelation and always means people who side with the beast against God. The souls under the altar ask God to “judge those who dwell upon the earth” (6:10); they gloat over the death of the two witnesses (11:10); and “all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast—all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain” (13:8). They are deceived by the false prophet and made drunk by Babylon. Set against them are those whose home is in heaven. Yet the judgments are meant to bring them to repentance, and an angel still carries an eternal gospel “to those who dwell on the earth” (14:6).
al: Those who dwell upon the earth
rel: Followers of the beast

sub: Harbor city of Asia, now Izmir
bio: A large harbor city north of Ephesus, now Izmir in Turkey, long loyal to Rome. The letter to Smyrna (Revelation 2:8-11) speaks of poverty, slander and coming prison, and promises “the crown of life” to those faithful to death.

sub: Royal city and center of emperor worship
bio: An old royal city on a steep hill, now Bergama in Turkey, with a great altar of Zeus and the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Roma. Christ says the church lives “where the throne of Satan sits” (Revelation 2:13).

A trading town of Lydia, now Akhisar in Turkey, known for its trade guilds. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth, came from here (Acts 16:14). The letter to Thyatira (Revelation 2:18-29) warns against the prophetess called Jezebel.
The old capital of Lydia, now Sart in Turkey, below an acropolis that twice fell by surprise. Christ says to the church, “you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead” (Revelation 3:1).
A city east of Sardis, now Alaşehir in Turkey, often shaken by earthquakes. The letter to Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7-13) has no rebuke and promises an open door that no one can shut.

n: The One seated on the throne
bio: In Revelation God is shown seated on the throne in heaven, shining like jasper and carnelian, with a rainbow around the throne (4:2-3). He is “the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come” (4:8), holds the sealed scroll (5:1), and at the end says, “Behold, I make all things new” (21:5). The book never describes his form.
al: He who sits on the throne
rel: Worshiped with the Lamb

sub: Messengers who carry out God’s will
bio: Angels fill the book: the seven angels who stand before God with trumpets (8:2), the angels who pour out the bowls (16:1), the mighty angel with the little scroll (10:1), the three angels who announce the gospel and judgment (14:6-11), and the angel who binds Satan (20:1). The star that had fallen from heaven and opens the Abyss (9:1) is also usually taken as an angel. An angel twice refuses John’s worship (19:10; 22:8-9).
rel: Servants of God and of the Lamb

sub: Locusts from the Abyss and unclean spirits
bio: Out of the smoke of the Abyss come locusts that torment people but not plants, with Abaddon as their king (9:1-11). At the sixth bowl three unclean spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast and the false prophet to gather the kings for battle (16:13-14).
rel: Serve the dragon

sub: Heaven, earth and sea in Revelation
bio: Every creature in heaven, on earth, under the earth and in the sea joins the praise of God and the Lamb (5:13). The earth, sea, rivers and sky are struck by the trumpets and bowls (8:7-12; 16:2-9), and at the end a new heaven and a new earth replace the first (21:1).
rel: Made by God, made new

sub: Peoples of the earth in Revelation
bio: John must prophesy “about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings” (10:11). The nations rage (11:18), drink Babylon’s wine (18:3), and are deceived by Satan (20:3, 8); yet the redeemed come from every nation (7:9), and in the new Jerusalem the nations walk by its light and bring their glory into it (21:24-26).
rel: Called to fear God and worship him

bio: Revelation calls God’s people saints and servants. Their prayers rise as incense (5:8; 8:3-4); the beast makes war on them (13:7); they are called to endurance and faithfulness (13:10; 14:12); a voice from heaven calls, “Come out of her, My people” (18:4); and the bride’s fine linen is “the righteous acts of the saints” (19:8).
rel: Servants of God and followers of the Lamb
